msc-12084-5043.introduction: is a hot Be star in Centaurus, about 410 light-years away, associated with the young Lower Centaurus–Crux population. Its bright primary is part of a wider multiple system.

sections.title: Gas around a rapid rotator
sections.text: Rapid rotation throws material off the star into a disk around its equator, giving it the distinctive spectrum of a shell star.

sections.title: Companions at different scales
sections.text: High-resolution observations reveal a close companion, with additional nearby stars sharing the system’s motion. Their wider relationships are less simple than the appearance of one bright catalog point suggests.

hip-27366.name: Saiph
hip-27366.introduction: is the blue supergiant at Orion’s southeastern corner, opposite Bellatrix, about 650 light-years away. It is smaller and less luminous than Rigel but hotter at its surface.

sections.title: A great deal of invisible light
sections.text: Its high temperature sends much of its energy into the ultraviolet. Comparing Saiph and Rigel by visible brightness alone therefore does not compare their total energy outputs.

sections.title: A brief supergiant phase
sections.text: Saiph’s strong wind carries off about the Sun’s mass every 1.1 million years. Like many of Orion’s bright stars, it is destined to collapse and explode as a supernova.

hip-107315.name: Enif
hip-107315.introduction: is the brightest star in Pegasus, marking the horse’s nose; its name is Arabic for “nose.” Although outside the Great Square, it outshines the Square’s stars.

sections.title: An unusually changeable beacon
sections.text: Enif is a slow irregular variable, but it was once seen very briefly at magnitude 0.7, raising the idea that supergiants may erupt in flares that dwarf the Sun’s.

sections.title: A huge, cool envelope
sections.text: With 11 to 12 times the Sun’s mass, Enif has swollen to 183 times the Sun’s radius. Its surface is cooler than the Sun’s, yet its vast size makes it intensely luminous.

msc-05320-0018.name: Mintaka
msc-05320-0018.introduction: is the westernmost star of Orion’s Belt, about 1,200 light-years away, and lies very close to the celestial equator. Its name comes from the Arabic for “belt.”

sections.title: A clockwork eclipse in the Belt
sections.text: The principal pair, a hot bright giant and a B-type star, orbits every 5.7 days and undergoes shallow eclipses. Johannes Hartmann established that period in 1904 from photographic plates taken at Potsdam.

sections.title: A hierarchy beyond the eclipse
sections.text: A third star orbits the eclipsing pair every 152 years, and a more distant visible companion is itself a 30-day binary: five hot, massive stars in all.

msc-05407-0157.name: Alnitak
msc-05407-0157.introduction: is the easternmost star of Orion’s Belt and the brightest O-type star in the night sky.

sections.title: A rare bright O star
sections.text: O stars are exceptionally hot and short-lived. Alnitak’s strong ultraviolet radiation and stellar wind make its environment very different from the quiet surroundings of a Sun-like star.

sections.title: Companions and neighboring clouds
sections.text: A close companion was found in 1998, after hints from interferometer observations in the 1970s, and another star lies farther out. The system is bathed in the glow of IC 434, near the famous Flame and Horsehead nebulae.

sections.title: A black hole in its future?
sections.text: In about a million years, Alnitak Aa should swell into a red supergiant wider than Jupiter’s orbit before exploding as a supernova, likely leaving a black hole.

hip-45556.name: Aspidiske
hip-45556.introduction: is the white supergiant Iota Carinae, a corner of the False Cross. Its name, like its Latin and Arabic counterparts, means “small shield.”

sections.title: A misleading cross
sections.text: Aspidiske, Avior, Markeb and Alsephina form the False Cross across Carina and Vela. Confusing it with Crux gives a misleading guide to the south celestial pole.

sections.title: Crossing toward cooler temperatures
sections.text: Aspidiske is an expanded A-type supergiant just entering the Hertzsprung gap, the sparsely populated stage between hot main-sequence stars and cool giants, on its way to becoming a red supergiant.

rigel.name: Rigel
rigel.introduction: is the brightest star in Orion and generally the seventh-brightest in the night sky: a blue supergiant about 850 light-years away, 61,500 to 363,000 times as luminous as the Sun, depending on the method used.

sections.title: A triple beside the supergiant
sections.text: Rigel B contains the close pair Ba and Bb, with C farther out. Together with the supergiant, they make a hierarchical four-star family whose components share one system story despite their very different brightnesses.

sections.title: A changing blue supergiant
sections.text: Rigel shows small pulsations and loses material through a stellar wind. Its changing light and spectrum let astronomers study the interior and atmosphere of a massive star in an advanced evolutionary phase.

sections.title: A future supernova
sections.text: Rigel is one of the closest known potential supernova progenitors. Its explosion could reach about magnitude −11, as bright as a quarter Moon, and leave a neutron star or black hole.

sections.title: Beta, not alpha
sections.text: Although Rigel usually outshines Betelgeuse, Johann Bayer designated it beta in 1603. One suggestion is that he did so during a rare period when the variable Betelgeuse was brighter.

hip-39429.name: Naos
hip-39429.introduction: is the brightest star in Puppis and one of the hottest and most luminous stars visible to the naked eye: an O-type supergiant more than 500,000 times as luminous as the Sun. Its name means “ship,” recalling the old constellation Argo Navis.

sections.title: A powerful stellar wind
sections.text: Naos drives a wind of about 2,500 km/s that strips more than a millionth of its mass each year, some 10 million times the Sun’s rate. Features moving through the wind show that it is far from smooth.

sections.title: A massive runaway
sections.text: Its motion identifies it as a runaway star. Proposed histories include binary interaction, a stellar merger or dynamical ejection; reconstructing the specific sequence is harder than establishing that it is moving unusually fast.

msc-08095-4720.name: Regor
msc-08095-4720.introduction: is the brightest star in Vela and contains by far the closest and brightest Wolf–Rayet star. It is also the brightest star without an IAU-approved name: neither Regor nor its traditional name Suhail al Muhlif is official.

sections.title: An exposed stellar interior
sections.text: The Wolf–Rayet star has lost much of its outer envelope, revealing material enriched by nuclear reactions. Its broad emission lines come from a dense, fast stellar wind.

sections.title: Winds crashing into winds
sections.text: The two massive stars circle every 78.5 days, between 0.8 and 1.6 AU apart. Where their winds collide, gas heats to X-ray temperatures, and the system also emits gamma rays in step with its orbit. Other members share its motion in the young Vela OB2 association.

sections.title: Roger, spelled backwards
sections.text: The name Regor, “Roger” reversed, honors Apollo 1 astronaut Roger Chaffee. It was coined in 1967 by the Apollo 9 crew and Clarence Cleminshaw; the popular story that Gus Grissom invented it as a joke is incorrect.

sections.title: Future supernovae
sections.text: Both the Wolf–Rayet star and its massive partner are likely to end their lives as supernovae, among the nearest candidates to the Sun.

hip-102098.name: Deneb
hip-102098.introduction: is the white supergiant at the tail of Cygnus and the head of the Northern Cross, and a corner of the Summer Triangle. If its largest distance estimates are right, it is the farthest star brighter than magnitude 2.5.

sections.title: A distance with consequences
sections.text: Deneb’s distance is uncertain, with estimates from 1,400 to 2,600 light-years, so its luminosity lies somewhere between 55,000 and 196,000 times the Sun’s.

sections.title: A subtly variable supergiant
sections.text: Small brightness and spectral changes make it the prototype of Alpha Cygni variables. Pulsations and its stellar wind provide clues to an advanced stage of massive-star evolution.

sections.title: A future pole star
sections.text: Around the year 9800, Earth’s precession will make Deneb an approximate pole star, about 7 degrees from the north celestial pole.

hip-34444.name: Wezen
hip-34444.introduction: is the yellow-white supergiant in Canis Major, about 1,600 light-years away. It appears less conspicuous than Sirius because it lies so much farther away. Since 1943 its spectrum has served as a standard for classifying other stars.

sections.title: A Sun-like temperature on a giant scale
sections.text: Its surface temperature is not far from the Sun’s, but with 14 to 15 times the Sun’s mass it has grown to about 190 times the Sun’s size.

sections.title: A short, massive life
sections.text: Wezen evolved rapidly because of its high mass. Once it develops an inert iron core, it will collapse and explode as a supernova.

hip-100453.name: Sadr
hip-100453.introduction: is the yellow-white supergiant at the crossing point of the Northern Cross, about 1,800 light-years away. Its name comes from the Arabic for “chest,” the same word behind Schedar in Cassiopeia.

sections.title: A star amid glowing clouds
sections.text: Sadr is surrounded by the diffuse glowing nebula IC 1318, also called the Gamma Cygni region.

sections.title: Near the pulsation strip
sections.text: Sadr’s spectrum and slow velocity changes place it near the realm of pulsating yellow supergiants. Its variations are more complicated than the regular cycle of a classical Cepheid.

hip-26311.name: Alnilam
hip-26311.introduction: is the middle star of Orion’s Belt, a blue supergiant about 1,250 light-years away and hundreds of thousands of times as luminous as the Sun. Its name comes from the Arabic for “arrangement” or “string of pearls.”

sections.title: A wind carrying matter away
sections.text: Alnilam’s winds reach up to 2,000 km/s, carrying off mass about 20 million times faster than the Sun loses it. Its relatively simple spectrum also makes it useful for studying interstellar gas.

sections.title: An apparent line across deep space
sections.text: Mintaka, Alnilam and Alnitak form a remarkably straight pattern from Earth, but their distances differ. Their similar apparent brightness conceals major differences in luminosity and system structure.

hip-35904.name: Aludra
hip-35904.introduction: is the blue supergiant Eta Canis Majoris, near the tail of the Great Dog, about 2,000 light-years away. Its name means “the virgin” in Arabic.

sections.title: A reference for supergiants
sections.text: Since 1943, its spectrum has been the standard for the B5 Ia class, an anchor for classifying hot, very luminous stars.

sections.title: A quietly changing light
sections.text: Aludra shows small variations characteristic of evolved supergiants. Its pulsations and wind reveal that even a seemingly steady constellation star can have a dynamic atmosphere and a changing energy output.

hip-25985.name: Arneb
hip-25985.introduction: is the yellow-white supergiant in Lepus, the Hare beneath Orion, with 12 to 13 times the Sun’s mass. Its name comes from the Arabic for “hare.”

sections.title: An enormous star below Orion
sections.text: Arneb’s radius is about 105 times the Sun’s: placed at the center of our Solar System, its surface would extend beyond Mercury’s orbit.

sections.title: A late stage with an uncertain route
sections.text: Its mass and evolved spectrum place it in a short-lived phase of stellar evolution. Whether such a star is crossing toward cooler temperatures or returning from a previous red-supergiant stage requires more than color alone to determine.

msc-08447-5443.name: Alsephina
msc-08447-5443.introduction: is the triple star Delta Velorum, about 81 light-years away and part of the False Cross. Its main pair is the brightest known eclipsing binary.

sections.title: Eclipses spotted from Jupiter
sections.text: The inner stars, Aa and Ab, orbit every 45 days. Their eclipses were announced in 2000, noticed independently by astronomers on the ground and by the Galileo spacecraft orbiting Jupiter. Interferometry first resolved the pair in 2007.

sections.title: A ship’s name
sections.text: Alsephina comes from the Arabic for “the ship,” originally a name for the whole constellation Argo Navis. The third star, B, circles the eclipsing pair every 143 years. Earth’s precession periodically carries Delta Velorum near the south celestial pole.

spectroscopic-hip-50583.name: Algieba
spectroscopic-hip-50583.introduction: is a pair of golden giants in Leo’s mane, part of the Sickle asterism. Its Arabic name means “the forehead,” although the star sits in the lion’s mane.

sections.title: A double for small telescopes
sections.text: William Herschel discovered in 1792 that Algieba is double; a modest telescope splits it into an orange-red and a yellowish giant. Both are probably about 2 billion years old and fusing helium in their cores. A 2025 orbit solution, based on 190 years of measurements, gives about 553 years per circuit. The flare star AD Leonis appears just 5 arcminutes away but is unrelated.

sections.title: A giant planet, or more
sections.text: In 2009 a gas giant was announced around the brighter star, on a 429-day orbit 1.2 AU out. A later analysis raised its minimum mass to about 10.7 Jupiter masses; if its orbit is seen far from edge-on, it may be massive enough to be a brown dwarf.

hip-35264.name: Ahadi
hip-35264.introduction: is Pi Puppis, an orange supergiant about 810 light-years away and the brightest star in the open cluster Collinder 135. Its informal name comes from the Arabic for “having much promise.”

sections.title: A short-lived giant
sections.text: With 11.7 times the Sun’s mass, it is only about 20 million years old yet has already swollen to about 235 times the Sun’s radius. It varies slightly, between magnitudes 2.70 and 2.85.

sections.title: A meteor shower nearby
sections.text: About every five years in late April, the Pi Puppids, a meteor shower linked to comet 26P/Grigg–Skjellerup, appear near the star.

hip-97278.name: Tarazed
hip-97278.introduction: is Gamma Aquilae, an orange bright giant about 395 light-years away, beside Altair. Its name comes from the Persian for “the scale beam,” describing the line it forms with Altair and Alshain.

sections.title: Old before its time
sections.text: Only about 270 million years old, Tarazed has already exhausted the hydrogen in its core. With 3.5 times the Sun’s mass, it has swollen to 92 times the Sun’s radius and now fuses helium; it will end as a white dwarf.

sections.title: Children of the Cowherd
sections.text: In the Chinese tale of the Cowherd and the Weaver Girl, Tarazed and Alshain are the children of Niulang (Altair) and Zhinü (Vega). The Koori people of Victoria saw the two as the black swan wives of Bunjil, the eagle Altair.

hip-65109.name: Kulou
hip-65109.introduction: is Iota Centauri, a white star about 59 light-years away with about twice the Sun’s mass. Its name, approved in 2025, comes from Kulou, the Arsenal, an ancient Chinese constellation dating back to the 2nd century BCE.

sections.title: Unusually dusty
sections.text: A debris disk lies within 6 AU of the star, and its dust is unusually bright for a star about 350 million years old, suggesting recent collisions among planetesimals. Kulou also seems to belong to the IC 2391 group of about 16 stars that share a common origin.

orb6-12417-0127-a-b.name: Porrima
orb6-12417-0127-a-b.introduction: is Gamma Virginis, a pair of nearly identical white stars about 38 light-years away. Its name is that of a Roman goddess of prophecy.

sections.title: A double that closes and opens
sections.text: The two stars orbit every 169 years on a very elongated path. Easy for amateur telescopes until the early 1990s, the pair then drew too close to split without larger instruments or special techniques; by 2020 the stars had separated enough for small telescopes again.

sections.title: On the Moon’s path
sections.text: Lying 2.8 degrees from the ecliptic, Porrima can be occulted by the Moon and, rarely, by planets; in June 2011 Saturn passed a quarter of a degree from it. Its X-ray emission suggests an age of about 1.1 billion years.

msc-16240+6131.name: Athebyne
msc-16240+6131.introduction: is Eta Draconis, the second-brightest star in Draco at only magnitude 2.7, about 92 light-years away. Its name means one of “the two wolves” of an Arabic sky picture, lying in wait for a camel’s foal together with Zeta Draconis.

sections.title: A giant and a distant companion
sections.text: Athebyne is a yellow giant with 2.9 times the Sun’s mass that reached this stage in only 650 million years, since massive stars burn through their hydrogen faster. A fainter orange dwarf, B, lies at least 140 AU away and needs at least a millennium to complete an orbit.

hip-86742.name: Cebalrai
hip-86742.introduction: is Beta Ophiuchi, an orange giant about 83 light-years away. Its name comes from the Arabic for “the shepherd’s dog.”

sections.title: An early giant
sections.text: Although only about 2.75 billion years old, 60% of the Sun’s age, it has expanded to about 12 times the Sun’s radius and radiates 58 times the Sun’s light. Small velocity changes every 142 days probably come from pulsations. The US Navy cargo ship USS Cheleb was named after the star.

msc-14509-1603.name: Zubenelgenubi
msc-14509-1603.introduction: is Alpha Librae, a quadruple star about 77 light-years away and, despite its alpha designation, only the second-brightest star in Libra. Its name means “the southern claw,” from the time when Libra’s stars belonged to Scorpius.

sections.title: Two pairs traveling together
sections.text: Its two bright members, α¹ and α² Librae, lie almost 4 arcminutes apart in the sky and move together through space. Each is itself a close binary; the two pairs are about 5,400 AU apart and probably belong to the Castor Moving Group.

sections.title: Hidden by the Moon
sections.text: Lying only 0.33 degrees from the ecliptic, α² can be occulted by the Moon and, very rarely, by planets: Venus covered it in 1947, and Mercury will in 2052.

hip-59747.name: Imai
hip-59747.introduction: is Delta Crucis, the faintest of the four bright stars of the Southern Cross, about 345 light-years away. Its name, adopted in 2018, comes from the Mursi people of Ethiopia.

sections.title: A calendar star
sections.text: For the Mursi, when Imai disappears from the evening sky around the end of August, the Omo River has risen high enough to flatten the imai grass along its banks. They use it with other southern stars to track the river’s seasonal floods.

sections.title: Hot, fast and on five flags
sections.text: A blue-white subgiant spinning at more than 210 km/s, Imai belongs to the 16–20-million-year-old Lower Centaurus–Crux group. As a star of the Southern Cross, it appears on the flags of Australia, New Zealand, Samoa and Papua New Guinea; on Brazil’s flag it represents Minas Gerais.

msc-10429-6423.name: Theta Carinae
msc-10429-6423.introduction: is the brightest star of IC 2602, the Southern Pleiades, about 460 light-years away, and marks one end of the Diamond Cross.

sections.title: A rejuvenated star
sections.text: Its primary, a hot B-type star of about 15 solar masses, looks much younger than its cluster: a blue straggler, probably rejuvenated by mass taken from its companion. The pair orbit in just 2.2 days, the shortest known period among massive stars.

msc-15351-4110.name: Gamma Lupi
msc-15351-4110.introduction: is a triple star in Lupus and a member of the young Upper Centaurus–Lupus association. In ancient Chinese astronomy, it was the first star of the Cavalry Officer.

sections.title: Three stars, two scales
sections.text: A close pair orbits every 2.85 days. The hotter star heats the facing side of its partner, so the light varies by about 0.02 magnitudes even without eclipses. A third star circles the pair about 81 AU out, taking 210 years.

orb6-16302+2129-aa-ab.name: Kornephoros
orb6-16302+2129-aa-ab.introduction: is Beta Herculis, the brightest star in Hercules, about 139 light-years away. Its name is Greek for “club bearer.”

sections.title: A wobble seen in 1899
sections.text: W. W. Campbell discovered in 1899 that its radial velocity varies, revealing a companion; speckle interferometry at Palomar resolved the pair in 1977. The two stars orbit every 410 days on an eccentric path.

sections.title: A future white dwarf
sections.text: The primary, a yellow giant with nearly three times the Sun’s mass, is probably fusing helium in its core; it resembles Capella’s main star but is warmer and brighter. Lacking the mass for a supernova, it will end as a white dwarf.

msc-17146+1423.name: Rasalgethi
msc-17146+1423.introduction: is Alpha Herculis, a red giant about 360 light-years away whose name means “head of the kneeler” in Arabic: Hercules was once drawn upside down. Five degrees away lies Rasalhague, perhaps the closest pair of alpha stars in the sky.

sections.title: A giant that breathes
sections.text: Rasalgethi A pulsates between about 264 and 303 times the Sun’s radius; placed at the Sun, it would reach beyond Earth’s orbit. It is the second-nearest asymptotic-giant-branch star to the Sun, losing gas into an envelope at least 930 AU across, and its brightness wanders between magnitudes 2.7 and 4.0.

sections.title: A triple system
sections.text: A telescope shows a companion, B, which is itself a yellow giant and a dwarf star orbiting every 51.6 days. A and B are more than 500 AU apart and take about 3,600 years per orbit.

hip-2021.name: Beta Hydri
hip-2021.introduction: is the brightest star in Hydrus, only about 24 light-years away, and the closest easily visible star to the south celestial pole. Around 150 BC it lay within two degrees of the pole, making it the southern pole star.

sections.title: A glimpse of the Sun’s future
sections.text: This subgiant has 113% of the Sun’s mass and is one of the oldest stars in the solar neighborhood, 6.1 to 7.5 billion years old. Running low on core hydrogen, it resembles what the Sun may look like in the distant future. Unusually for an evolved star, it has a strong magnetic field, apparently regenerated during its subgiant phase.

sections.title: A planet that faded
sections.text: A long-term trend reported in 2002 hinted at a Jupiter-like planet, but later measurements attributed the variations to the star’s magnetic cycle.

hip-63608.name: Vindemiatrix
hip-63608.introduction: is Epsilon Virginis, the third-brightest star in Virgo, about 110 light-years away. Its name means “the grape-harvester” in Latin.

sections.title: A helium-burning giant
sections.text: With 2.7 times the Sun’s mass and an age of 700 million years, it is probably a red clump giant fusing helium in its core, at 12 times the Sun’s size. Since 1943, its spectrum has served as a standard for classifying other stars.

sections.title: The Barker
sections.text: Arab astronomers grouped it with Zavijava, Porrima, Zaniah and Minelauva as al-ʽAwwāʼ, “the Barker.”

hip-23875.name: Cursa
hip-23875.introduction: is Beta Eridani, the second-brightest star in Eridanus, about 89 light-years away at the river’s northern end near Orion. Its name comes from the Arabic for “the chair” or “footstool” of the central one.

sections.title: A fast-spinning giant
sections.text: This white giant spins at about 196 km/s, nearly 100 times the speed of the Sun’s equator. Its brightness varies slightly, and a particularly strong flare-up was reported in 1985. It may belong to the Ursa Major supergroup, although its properties suggest it could be an interloper.

hip-85670.name: Rastaban
hip-85670.introduction: is Beta Draconis, a yellow bright giant in the dragon’s head, about 380 light-years away. Its name comes from the Arabic for “head of the serpent.”

sections.title: A young giant
sections.text: Only about 65 million years old, Rastaban has six times the Sun’s mass and about 40 times its radius. It is a spectral standard for its class, and its strong chromosphere emits X-rays and far-ultraviolet light. A faint dwarf companion orbits it roughly once every four thousand years.

sections.title: The Mother Camels
sections.text: With Eltanin and other stars of Draco’s head, it formed the Arabic asterism of the Mother Camels.

hip-90496.name: Kaus Borealis
hip-90496.introduction: is Lambda Sagittarii, the top of the archer’s bow and part of the Teapot, about 78 light-years away. Its name combines the Arabic for “bow” and the Latin for “northern.” It is an orange giant with 1.8 times the Sun’s mass.

sections.title: Planets pass in front
sections.text: Lying 2.1 degrees from the ecliptic, it is sometimes occulted by the Moon and, rarely, by planets: Venus covered it in 1984 and Mercury in 1865. On December 17, 2021, Mercury passed within an arcminute of it.

hip-81266.name: Paikauhale
hip-81266.introduction: is Tau Scorpii, a hot blue-white star about 470 light-years away, just south of Antares. Its name is Hawaiian, meaning a wanderer going from house to house.

sections.title: A magnetic star
sections.text: With 15 times the Sun’s mass, it radiates about 25,000 times the Sun’s light. Its magnetic field has been mapped across its surface, and its unusually hard X-rays suggest clumps of plasma falling onto the star. It rotates slowly, once in 41 days.

sections.title: Tomorrow’s Antares
sections.text: Only about 5 million years old, it should leave the main sequence in about 5.4 million years and, about a million years later, become a red supergiant comparable to Antares.

sections.title: Arteries of the scorpion
sections.text: Arab astronomers called it and Sigma Scorpii “the arteries,” flanking Antares, the scorpion’s heart. In Hawaiian tradition, it forms a line of three stars with Antares and Sigma Scorpii.

hip-39757.name: Tureis
hip-39757.introduction: is Rho Puppis, a yellow-white bright giant about 64 light-years away and the prototype of the Rho Puppis class of evolved, chemically peculiar stars. Its name comes from the Arabic for “small shield.”

sections.title: An early pulsator
sections.text: Olin Eggen announced its variability in 1956, making it one of the first Delta Scuti stars identified; it pulsates 7.1 times a day. In 2017 it became only the second Delta Scuti star known to have a magnetic field.

sections.title: A past close pass
sections.text: About 394,000 years ago it came within roughly 11.6 light-years of the Sun, about Procyon’s distance today. Cold dust about 50 AU from the star suggests a debris disk.

hip-110130.name: Lang-Exster
hip-110130.introduction: is Alpha Tucanae, the brightest star in Tucana, about 184 light-years away: an orange giant 37 times the Sun’s diameter with an unseen companion.

sections.title: A double name
sections.text: Approved in 2024, the name combines the Malay and Indonesian word for hornbill with the Dutch word for magpie, both former names for the constellation. Because the star is a binary, it received a double name.

sections.title: An unseen partner
sections.text: The companion has never been seen directly; it reveals itself through shifts in the giant’s spectrum, completing an orbit every 11.5 years.

hip-107556.name: Deneb Algedi
hip-107556.introduction: is Delta Capricorni, the brightest star in Capricornus, about 39 light-years away, marking the sea-goat’s tail; its name is Arabic for “tail of the goat.” It is the closest known eclipsing binary.

sections.title: Eclipses every day
sections.text: Its two stars orbit in just over a day, dimming the system from magnitude 2.81 to 3.05 and 2.90 during the two eclipses. Vesto Slipher found the binary in 1906, but the eclipses were not discovered until 1956.

sections.title: On the Moon’s path
sections.text: Lying 2.6 degrees from the ecliptic, it can be occulted by the Moon; occultations were observed in 1951, 1962 and 1988.

hip-25606.name: Nihal
hip-25606.introduction: is Beta Leporis, the second-brightest star in Lepus, about 160 light-years away. Its name comes from the Arabic for “quenching their thirst.”

sections.title: A young bright giant
sections.text: With 3.5 times the Sun’s mass, Nihal is about 240 million years old, long enough to become a yellow bright giant about 16 times the Sun’s radius. A fainter companion lies 2.6 arcseconds away and may be bound to it.

hip-9236.name: Alpha Hydri
hip-9236.introduction: is the second-brightest star in Hydrus, about 72 light-years away, sometimes called the Head of Hydrus and not to be confused with Alphard in Hydra. It is easy to find south and east of Achernar.

sections.title: A young subgiant
sections.text: About 810 million years old, it has 2.1 times the Sun’s mass and 3.3 times its size, and it emits X-rays much like Altair.

hip-1067.name: Algenib
hip-1067.introduction: is Gamma Pegasi, the southeast corner of the Great Square of Pegasus, about 470 light-years away. Its name was once also used for Mirfak in Perseus.

sections.title: A hybrid pulsator
sections.text: Algenib is a Beta Cephei variable that pulsates every 3.6 hours, while also showing the slower pulsations of another class of B stars, so it is called a hybrid pulsator. Its changing velocity was first noticed in 1911, and in 2025 interferometry revealed a close companion.

sections.title: Seen from Artemis II
sections.text: Algenib appeared in photographs of the Sun eclipsed by the Moon taken during the Artemis II mission in April 2026.

hip-77952.name: Beta Trianguli Australis
hip-77952.introduction: is the second-brightest star in Triangulum Australe, about 40 light-years away. The Wardaman people of Australia call it Jirradella, “rainbow sign.”

sections.title: A dusty young neighbor?
sections.text: This F-type star shows excess infrared light, a hint of circumstellar debris. It may belong to the Beta Pictoris moving group, which would make it only about 12 million years old. On Brazil’s flag, it represents the state of Santa Catarina.

hip-85258.name: Beta Arae
hip-85258.introduction: is the brightest star in Ara, the Altar, about 710 light-years away: an orange supergiant 141 times the Sun’s size and 5,800 times as luminous.

sections.title: Embers in the altar
sections.text: About 50 million years old, it spent most of its life as a hot B-type star before swelling to its current size, and it has more than three times the Sun’s abundance of heavy elements. A rare Turkish name means “middle of the embers,” fitting a constellation that Arabic calls the incense burner.

hip-18246.name: Zeta Persei
hip-18246.introduction: is a blue-white supergiant in Perseus, roughly 850 to 1,300 light-years away, and a member of the young Perseus OB2 association.

sections.title: A massive star with a strong wind
sections.text: With 13 to 16 times the Sun’s mass and about 47,000 times its luminosity, it blows a wind that carries off the Sun’s mass every 4.3 million years. Its spectrum shows unusually high carbon. A 9th-magnitude star with the same motion may be a companion at least 4,000 AU away.

sections.title: A shared name
sections.text: It once shared the name Atik, “the collarbone of the Pleiades,” with Omicron Persei; the IAU has since assigned Atik to Omicron Persei.

hip-30343.name: Tejat
hip-30343.introduction: is Mu Geminorum, a red giant in Gemini, about 230 light-years away. Lying less than a degree from the ecliptic, it can be occulted by the Moon and, rarely, by planets.

sections.title: A late-stage giant
sections.text: Tejat has expanded to more than 100 times the Sun’s size and is over 1,500 times as luminous. On the asymptotic giant branch, it fuses hydrogen and helium in shells around an inert carbon–oxygen core, and it varies irregularly between magnitudes 2.75 and 3.02. Its name comes from an old southern Arabic word of unknown meaning.

hip-17702.name: Alcyone
hip-17702.introduction: is the brightest star of the Pleiades, about 440 light-years away, named after one of the seven daughters of Atlas and Pleione in Greek myth.

sections.title: A spinning Be star
sections.text: Alcyone is a blue-white giant spinning so fast that it is visibly oblate: about 10.6 times the Sun’s radius at the equator but 8 at the poles. Like many Be stars, it has flung a disk of gas from its equator.

sections.title: Younger than its cluster?
sections.text: The Pleiades are about 130 million years old, but Alcyone appears younger and may be a blue straggler. Kepler data revealed tiny brightness changes, the strongest repeating every 2.3 days, probably its rotation.

orb6-19450+4508-a-b.name: Fawaris
orb6-19450+4508-a-b.introduction: is Delta Cygni, a triple star on the crossbar of the Northern Cross, about 165 light-years away. Its name comes from the Arabic asterism “the Riders,” formed with Zeta, Epsilon and Gamma Cygni.

sections.title: Three stars
sections.text: A blue-white giant spinning at least 135 km/s and a yellow-white companion orbit each other every 780 years, about 157 AU apart. A faint orange star travels with them.

sections.title: A future pole star
sections.text: For at least four centuries around the year 11,250, Earth’s precession will make Delta Cygni a pole star.

hip-13847.name: Acamar
hip-13847.introduction: is Theta Eridani, a triple star about 167 light-years away. Its name comes from the Arabic for “the end of the river,” via a misreading that turned “rn” into “m.”

sections.title: Two stars become three
sections.text: A telescope splits Acamar into two white stars 8.3 arcseconds apart. The brighter, θ¹, is itself a pair orbiting every 4.1 days, so close that tides distort their shapes; the VLT’s GRAVITY instrument resolved it directly in 2025.

sections.title: Brighter in antiquity
sections.text: Ptolemy and al-Sufi listed it among the brightest stars in the sky. One explanation is a millennium-long outburst powered by mass transfer between the stars of θ¹.

msc-12560+3819.name: Cor Caroli
msc-12560+3819.introduction: is Alpha Canum Venaticorum, the brightest star in Canes Venatici, about 110 light-years away, and a double easily split with a small telescope. Its name means “Charles’s Heart.”

sections.title: Which Charles?
sections.text: Sir Charles Scarborough coined the name in 1660, claiming the star shone especially brightly the night Charles II returned to England. Yet the first star map to show it, Francis Lamb’s chart of 1673, called it the heart of “Charles the martyred king,” Charles I.

sections.title: A magnetic prototype
sections.text: The brighter star has a magnetic field about 5,000 times Earth’s and an atmosphere rich in silicon, mercury and europium. Enormous starspots make its brightness vary every 5.47 days, and it is the prototype of the Alpha² Canum Venaticorum variables. The two stars, about 650 AU apart, take around 8,000 years per orbit.

hip-36188.name: Gomeisa
hip-36188.introduction: is Beta Canis Minoris, a blue-white Be star about 162 light-years away, near Procyon. Its name comes from the Arabic for “the bleary-eyed one.”

sections.title: A spinning star with a disk
sections.text: With 3.5 times the Sun’s mass, it rotates at least 210 km/s, perhaps once a day, and is surrounded by a thin disk of gas about three times its radius. The MOST space telescope found tiny pulsations repeating about three times a day.

sections.title: A possible stripped companion
sections.text: It probably has a companion on a 170-day orbit, with about 42% of the Sun’s mass; one idea is a hot subdwarf left behind after the two stars interacted and spun up Gomeisa.

msc-03579+4001.name: Epsilon Persei
msc-03579+4001.introduction: is a hot blue-white star in Perseus, about 640 light-years away, with 12 to 16 times the Sun’s mass. Its proper name, Áldu, approved in December 2025, is the Sámi word for a female reindeer.

sections.title: A Sámi reindeer
sections.text: In Sámi tradition, it is part of Sarvvis, a great reindeer or moose spanning Cassiopeia, Perseus and Auriga, hunted by Fávdna, the star Arcturus.

sections.title: Companions and pulsations
sections.text: A close companion orbits every 14 days on an eccentric path, and a third body may orbit every 26 years. The primary, a standard star for class B0.5 III, is a Beta Cephei variable pulsating about six times a day. A 9th-magnitude star 9 arcseconds away shares its motion.

hip-74946.name: Gamma Trianguli Australis
hip-74946.introduction: is the third star of the Southern Triangle, about 190 light-years away: a white giant spinning at about 199 km/s.

sections.title: Dust and a doubtful companion
sections.text: Cold dust about 480 AU from the star suggests a debris disk. Gaia data hinted at a red-dwarf companion on a 488-day orbit, but VLT observations found no sign of it. On Brazil’s flag, it represents the state of Paraná.

hip-106278.name: Sadalsuud
hip-106278.introduction: is Beta Aquarii, the brightest star in Aquarius, a yellow supergiant about 540 light-years away. Its name comes from the Arabic for “luck of lucks.”

sections.title: A supergiant that will fade quietly
sections.text: About 56 million years old, with five or six times the Sun’s mass, it has grown to 48 times the Sun’s radius. It cannot explode as a supernova and will likely end as a massive white dwarf like Sirius B. Chandra detected X-rays from its corona, among the first from a yellow supergiant.

sections.title: A trio heading out of the plane
sections.text: Sadalsuud, Sadalmelik and Matar move together almost perpendicular to the plane of the Milky Way. Since 1943, Sadalsuud’s spectrum has been a classification standard, and it is also an IAU radial-velocity standard.

zeta-herculis.name: Zeta Herculis
zeta-herculis.introduction: is a pair of Sun-like stars in Hercules, only about 35 light-years away. Its proper name, Tianji, adopted in 2026, comes from the Chinese asterism “Celestial Discipline.”

sections.title: An evolving Sun
sections.text: The primary is a subgiant with 1.45 times the Sun’s mass that has just begun to leave the main sequence; its companion is about the Sun’s size and mass. They orbit every 34.45 years, about 15 AU apart. Friedrich Struve reported the pair in 1826.

sections.title: A moving group
sections.text: The system gives its name to the Zeta Herculis moving group, which also includes Zeta Reticuli and Phi² Pavonis.

msc-15589-2607.name: Fang
msc-15589-2607.introduction: is Pi Scorpii, a triple star about 590 light-years away in the young Upper Scorpius association.

sections.title: Two hot stars in a day and a half
sections.text: Edward Pickering announced in 1899 that it is double. The two hot B stars orbit in 1.57 days, only about 15 solar radii apart, and their mutual distortion and shallow eclipses vary the light slightly. A faint third star lies at least 7,000 AU away.

spectroscopic-hip-14328.name: Gamma Persei
spectroscopic-hip-14328.introduction: is a giant star in Perseus, about 221 light-years away, near the radiant of the Perseid meteor shower, about 4 degrees to its north.

sections.title: A rare eclipse
sections.text: It is a wide eclipsing binary with a 14.6-year orbit. The first eclipse was observed in 1990 and lasted two weeks, dimming the system by 0.55 magnitudes.

sections.title: A merged giant?
sections.text: The companion appears much older than the giant, so the giant is probably the product of a stellar merger, its apparent age measuring only the time since two stars combined.

hip-32768.name: Tau Puppis
hip-32768.introduction: is an orange giant in Puppis, about 182 light-years away, near the border with Carina.

sections.title: A partner in the spectrum
sections.text: H. D. Curtis and H. K. Palmer detected its changing velocity in 1908; a companion orbits every 2.9 years. Interferometry puts the giant at about 27 times the Sun’s radius. Its traditional Arabic name, Bulqayn, is of unknown meaning.

hip-109074.name: Sadalmelik
hip-109074.introduction: is Alpha Aquarii, a yellow supergiant about 520 to 760 light-years away, just marginally fainter than Sadalsuud. Its name comes from the Arabic for “the lucky star of the king,” and it lies within a degree of the celestial equator.

sections.title: A cool supergiant
sections.text: About 53 million years old, it has grown to 70 times the Sun’s radius and radiates 3,900 times the Sun’s light; like Sadalsuud, it will likely end as a massive white dwarf. A supersonic wind flows from its chromosphere, and Chandra found it unusually faint in X-rays, a common trait of early G-type giants.

hip-60965.name: Algorab
hip-60965.introduction: is Delta Corvi, a white star about 87 light-years away whose name is Arabic for “the crow.” Medieval astrologers counted it among the Behenian fixed stars.

sections.title: Young or nearly done?
sections.text: It is brighter than a main-sequence star of its type, so it is either a 260-million-year-old subgiant leaving the main sequence or a 3-million-year-old star still settling onto it. James South and John Herschel recorded its 9th-magnitude companion in 1823.

spectroscopic-hip-112158.name: Matar
spectroscopic-hip-112158.introduction: is Eta Pegasi, a yellow bright giant about 214 light-years away. Its name comes from the Arabic for “lucky star of rain.”

sections.title: A slow-turning giant
sections.text: The giant has 3.5 times the Sun’s mass and 24 times its radius; it slowed as it expanded and now rotates about once in 818 days. A white F-type companion orbits it every 813 days.

hip-85792.name: Alpha Arae
hip-85792.introduction: is a hot Be star in Ara, about 270 light-years away, spinning close to its breakup speed.

sections.title: A disk seen by interferometry
sections.text: Its equator moves at about 470 km/s, giving it a pronounced bulge. VLT interferometry in 2003 and 2005 showed a dense disk of gas orbiting its equator and a polar wind of about 1,000 km/s.

sections.title: Choo
sections.text: In Chinese astronomy, it belongs to the Pestle asterism; Patrick Moore listed Choo as a proper name for the star.

hip-47908.name: Epsilon Leonis
hip-47908.introduction: is a yellow giant in the lion’s head, about 247 light-years away. Its names, Algenubi and Ras Elased Australis, both mean “the southern star of the lion’s head.”

sections.title: Brighter than it looks
sections.text: It appears fainter than Regulus only because it is more than three times farther away; its absolute magnitude is significantly brighter. It varies by a few tenths of a magnitude every few days, like a Cepheid.

hip-32246.name: Mebsuta
hip-32246.introduction: is Epsilon Geminorum, a yellow supergiant about 860 light-years away on Castor’s outstretched leg. Its name refers to the outstretched paw of a vast lion in an ancient Arabian sky picture.

sections.title: Measured by CHARA
sections.text: The CHARA array measured its radius directly at 137 times the Sun’s. It has 5.3 times the Sun’s mass, is about 100 million years old, and has served as a classification standard since 1943.

sections.title: Occulted by Mars
sections.text: Lying near the ecliptic, it can be occulted by the Moon or planets. When Mars passed in front of it on April 8, 1976, astronomers used the event to measure the oblateness of the planet’s outer atmosphere; the asteroid Iphigenia occulted it in 2015.

hip-59316.name: Minkar
hip-59316.introduction: is Epsilon Corvi, an orange giant about 318 light-years away. Its name comes from the Arabic for the crow’s “beak.”

sections.title: Once a blue star
sections.text: With about three times the Sun’s mass, it spent most of its life as a hot B-type star before expanding to 57 times the Sun’s radius.

msc-16519-3803.name: Xamidimura
msc-16519-3803.introduction: is Mu¹ Scorpii, an eclipsing binary about 500 light-years away. Its name comes from the Khoekhoe for “the eyes of the lion,” the Khoikhoi name for Mu¹ and Mu² Scorpii.

sections.title: An early eclipsing binary
sections.text: Solon Bailey discovered in 1896 that it is a spectroscopic binary, only the third such eclipsing pair then known. Two hot B stars orbit in 34 hours 43 minutes, only 12.9 solar radii apart; the smaller nearly fills, or overflows, its share of space.

hip-88635.name: Alnasl
hip-88635.introduction: is Gamma² Sagittarii, an orange giant at the tip of the archer’s arrow and part of the Teapot, about 106 light-years away. Its name comes from the Arabic for “arrowhead.”

sections.title: Ostriches and swallows
sections.text: Arab astronomers saw an ostrich going down to drink from the Milky Way, with Alnasl as its first star; to the Akkadians, it and two neighbors formed the Swallow. Gamma¹ Sagittarii, about 50 arcminutes away, is an unrelated Cepheid variable.

sections.title: A helium-burning giant
sections.text: With twice the Sun’s mass, it has expanded to about 12 times the Sun’s radius and now fuses helium in its core.

msc-06203-3004.name: Furud
msc-06203-3004.introduction: is Zeta Canis Majoris, a blue-white star about 362 light-years away. Its name comes from the Arabic for “the solitary ones,” which early Arab poets used for anonymous stars.

sections.title: An unseen partner
sections.text: G. E. Paddock noticed its binary nature in 1906; the companion, never seen directly, orbits every 675 days on an elongated path. The primary has nearly eight times the Sun’s mass and is about 32 million years old. Furud lies close to the solar antapex, the direction the Sun is moving away from.

hip-93747.name: Okab
hip-93747.introduction: is Zeta Aquilae, a white star about 83 light-years away marking the eagle’s tail; with Epsilon Aquilae, it once bore the Arabic name for “the tail of the eagle.”

sections.title: A spinning reference star
sections.text: It rotates at more than 306 km/s, flattening it to 2.76 solar radii at the equator and 2.15 at the poles, and we see it almost edge-on. Astronomers use it as a telluric standard, to remove the imprint of Earth’s atmosphere from spectra of other stars. It may belong to the TW Hydrae association.

hip-87073.name: Iota¹ Scorpii
hip-87073.introduction: is a highly luminous yellow-white supergiant in Scorpius, about 1,930 light-years away and 35,000 times as luminous as the Sun.

sections.title: A distant giant
sections.text: With 12 times the Sun’s mass and 120 times its radius, it shines at third magnitude despite its distance and the interstellar dust that dims it by 0.66 magnitudes. A 10th-magnitude companion lies at least 20,000 AU away.

orb6-02095+3459-a-b.name: Alaybasan
orb6-02095+3459-a-b.introduction: is Beta Trianguli, the brightest star in Triangulum, about 127 light-years away, though only of third magnitude. Its name, approved in 2025, comes from the Arabic for “the two joints,” a name it once shared with Mothallah, Alpha Trianguli.

sections.title: Two giants and a ring of dust
sections.text: Two A-type giants orbit every 31.4 days on an eccentric path. The system was one of the steadiest stars Hipparcos observed, varying by only 0.0005 magnitudes, and Spitzer found a ring of dust around both stars extending from 50 to 400 AU.

hip-64962.name: Gamma Hydrae
hip-64962.introduction: is the second-brightest star in Hydra, a yellow giant about 134 light-years away.

sections.title: Old at a young age
sections.text: With nearly three times the Sun’s mass, it has reached an advanced stage of evolution at only about 372 million years old, because massive stars burn their fuel faster. A smaller companion of about 60% of the Sun’s mass lies 1.6 arcseconds away; radial velocities confirm that the two are bound.

hip-75097.name: Pherkad
hip-75097.introduction: is Gamma Ursae Minoris, one of the two “Guardians of the Pole” at the end of the Little Dipper’s bowl, about 487 light-years away. Its name comes from the Arabic for “calf,” from a phrase meaning “the dim one of the two calves,” the other being Kochab.

sections.title: A shell star in transition
sections.text: Pherkad is a white giant 15 times the Sun’s radius and 1,100 times as luminous, spinning at least 180 km/s with a disk of gas around its equator. Stellar models suggest it may become a Cepheid variable before turning into a red giant like Kochab and finally a white dwarf.

hip-108085.name: Aldhanab
hip-108085.introduction: is Gamma Gruis, a blue-white star about 211 light-years away in Grus, a region of sky that once belonged to Ptolemy’s Piscis Austrinus.

sections.title: A very wide companion
sections.text: It radiates about 390 times the Sun’s luminosity, much of it as ultraviolet light. A small star with about 30% of the Sun’s mass shares its motion and distance some 162,000 AU away, about 2.6 light-years, and the two likely form a binary.

hip-54539.name: Psi Ursae Majoris
hip-54539.introduction: is an orange giant in Ursa Major, about 140 light-years away, that has expanded to about 20 times the Sun’s radius.

sections.title: A calm galactic orbit
sections.text: It follows a nearly circular path around the Milky Way, never straying more than about 130 light-years from the galactic plane.

hip-17358.name: Delta Persei
hip-17358.introduction: is a blue-white star in Perseus, about 520 light-years away, and possibly a member of the Alpha Persei Cluster, where it would be the second-brightest star after Mirfak. Its proper name, Sarvvis, comes from a Sámi constellation.

sections.title: A runaway with a bow wave
sections.text: With about seven times the Sun’s mass and an age of only 6.8 million years, it spins at least 190 km/s. It moves at more than 30 km/s relative to its surroundings, making it a runaway star, and infrared images show a ring-like bow wave around it. It is probably binary, perhaps triple.

sections.title: The Sámi reindeer
sections.text: In Sámi tradition, Sarvvis is a great reindeer or moose spanning Cassiopeia, Perseus and Auriga, hunted by Fávdna, the star Arcturus. Nearby Epsilon Persei carries the name Áldu, a female reindeer.

hip-71075.name: Seginus
hip-71075.introduction: is Gamma Boötis, a white star at the herdsman’s left shoulder, about 86 light-years away.

sections.title: A pulsating star with a dusty ring
sections.text: Seginus is a Delta Scuti variable, pulsating about every 7 hours; its variability was discovered in 1914. It spins at 115 to 145 km/s, and a cold dust disk orbits about 99 AU out. A close companion was discovered in 1975, while a faint star 33 arcseconds away is a distant background object.

hip-33977.name: Omicron² Canis Majoris
hip-33977.introduction: is a blue supergiant in Canis Major, about 3,600 light-years away and one of the most luminous stars known, radiating about 220,000 times as much light as the Sun.

sections.title: A star destined to explode
sections.text: With about 24 times the Sun’s mass and 65 times its radius, it will probably end its life as a supernova. It is an Alpha Cygni variable whose brightness cycles over 24.4 days, and since 1943 it has served as a standard for spectral classification. Its neighbor in the sky, Omicron¹ Canis Majoris, is not physically related.

hip-26451.name: Tianguan
hip-26451.introduction: is Zeta Tauri, a hot Be star in Taurus about 440 light-years away. Lying near the ecliptic, it can be occulted by the Moon.

sections.title: A spiral in its disk
sections.text: The primary, with more than 11 times the Sun’s mass, is surrounded by a disk of gas thrown off by its rapid spin. A one-armed spiral wave runs through the disk, perhaps stirred by the companion, which orbits every 133 days about 1.2 AU away. One idea is that the companion is a white dwarf feeding on that material, which would explain the system’s hard X-rays.

msc-12463-6806.name: Beta Muscae
msc-12463-6806.introduction: is the second-brightest star in Musca, about 340 light-years away: two hot B-type stars of about 7.4 and 6.4 solar masses that orbit each other every 194 years.

sections.title: A runaway pair
sections.text: The system belongs to the Scorpius–Centaurus association, yet moves at about 44 km/s relative to normal galactic rotation, making it a runaway; binaries make up only a small fraction of runaway stars.

msc-10223+4130.name: Tania Australis
msc-10223+4130.introduction: is Mu Ursae Majoris, a red giant about 230 light-years away. Its name combines the Arabic for “the second spring of the gazelle” with the Latin australis, “southern.”

sections.title: A giant and its close partner
sections.text: The giant has expanded to 75 times the Sun’s radius. A companion orbits only 0.2 AU away every 230 days, and a tiny star of about 0.1 solar masses, 3,900 AU out, is very likely part of the system too.

hip-94376.name: Altais
hip-94376.introduction: is Delta Draconis, a yellow giant about 98 light-years away. Its name comes from the Arabic for “the goat.”

sections.title: A future white dwarf
sections.text: About 1.7 billion years old, with 1.7 times the Sun’s mass, it has expanded to 10.5 times the Sun’s radius and will end its life as a white dwarf.

hip-83081.name: Zeta Arae
hip-83081.introduction: is an orange giant or supergiant in Ara, about 490 light-years away, 114 times the Sun’s size.

sections.title: A possible distant companion
sections.text: With 7 to 8 times the Sun’s mass, it radiates 3,800 times the Sun’s light. A candidate companion announced in 2022 lies about 20,600 AU away.

msc-19307+2758.name: Albireo
msc-19307+2758.introduction: is the head of Cygnus, the swan, and one of the most beautiful double stars in the sky: an amber star and a blue-green companion, easy to split with a small telescope.

sections.title: A colorful contrast
sections.text: The brighter star, at magnitude 3.1, is amber, and the fainter, at 5.1, blue-green, 35 arcseconds apart, giving one of the best color contrasts in the sky. The amber star is itself a close triple system.

sections.title: A mysterious name
sections.text: The name Albireo may come from a garbled Latin phrase in a medieval translation of Ptolemy’s Almagest, with an “l” later added as if it were Arabic. Medieval Arab astronomers called the star “the hen’s beak.”

msc-20210-1447.name: Dabih
msc-20210-1447.introduction: is Beta Capricorni, a multiple star of perhaps five members about 390 light-years away, which binoculars split into two. Its name comes from the Arabic for “the butcher.”

sections.title: Two families of stars
sections.text: The brighter, Beta¹, is an orange giant with a close pair orbiting it every 3.8 years; that pair’s own stars circle each other in 8.7 days. The fainter, Beta², is also a binary. The two groups lie at least 21,000 AU apart and, if bound, take about a million years per orbit. Lying near the ecliptic, Beta Capricorni can be occulted by the Moon.

hip-43813.name: Zeta Hydrae
hip-43813.introduction: is a yellow giant in Hydra, about 157 light-years away, and the third-brightest star of the constellation.

sections.title: A neighbor of Delta Hydrae
sections.text: It lies about 12.9 light-years from Delta Hydrae and may move together with it. With 3.1 times the Sun’s mass and an age of about 370 million years, it has grown to 17.6 times the Sun’s radius, as measured by interferometry. On Groote Eylandt, its star group was Unwala, “the Crab.”

hip-89642.name: Eta Sagittarii
hip-89642.introduction: is a red giant in Sagittarius, about 146 light-years away. Its proper name, Heryibwia, adopted in 2026, comes from an ancient Egyptian star name meaning “the star in the middle of the boat.”

sections.title: An aging giant
sections.text: Having exhausted both hydrogen and helium in its core, it is on the asymptotic giant branch, about 57 times the Sun’s radius. A companion first noted by S. W. Burnham in 1879 lies at least 165 AU away, taking over 1,270 years per orbit. Its motion will carry it into Corona Australis around 6300 CE.

hip-52943.name: Nu Hydrae
hip-52943.introduction: is an orange giant in Hydra, about 137 light-years away, once designated 4 Crateris.

sections.title: A fast neighbor
sections.text: It has expanded to 21 times the Sun’s radius and has about half the Sun’s abundance of heavy elements. Its peculiar velocity is roughly three times that of its neighbors.

msc-14592-4206.name: Kappa Centauri
msc-14592-4206.introduction: is a triple star in Centaurus, about 400 light-years away, in the Upper Centaurus–Lupus association.

sections.title: Three stars
sections.text: Two hot B stars of 8.4 and 4.4 solar masses orbit each other every 58 years, seen almost edge-on. An orange dwarf circles them 3.9 arcseconds away, taking an estimated 3,200 years.

hip-101772.name: Alpha Indi
hip-101772.introduction: is the brightest star in Indus, an orange giant about 100 light-years away.

sections.title: A giant and two possible companions
sections.text: About 1.6 billion years old, with 2.15 times the Sun’s mass, it has grown to 9.9 times the Sun’s radius. Two red dwarfs at least 2,000 AU away may be companions. With Peacock, it formed the Arabic asterism of the Two Shrikes.

hip-27628.name: Wazn
hip-27628.introduction: is Beta Columbae, an orange giant about 87 light-years away. Its name comes from the Arabic for “weight.” Despite its 11.5 times larger radius, it has only about 10% more mass than the Sun.

sections.title: A close pass by Beta Pictoris
sections.text: Wazn races through space at about 100 km/s relative to the Sun. About 107,200 years ago it passed within roughly 1.9 light-years of Beta Pictoris and may have disturbed the outer planetesimals of that star’s famous debris disk.

msc-17150+2450.name: Sarin
msc-17150+2450.introduction: is Delta Herculis, a white star about 75 light-years away; the name Sarin first appeared in a 20th-century star atlas.

sections.title: A star and its close partner
sections.text: With about twice the Sun’s mass and radius, it radiates about 18.5 times the Sun’s light. Its close companion, Ab, is about 1.3 magnitudes fainter.

msc-08592+4803.name: Talitha
msc-08592+4803.introduction: is Iota Ursae Majoris, a star system about 47 light-years away. Its name comes from the Arabic for “the third leap of the gazelle.”

sections.title: Two pairs on an unstable course
sections.text: The bright white subgiant has an unseen companion, probably a white dwarf, on an 11-year orbit. A pair of red dwarfs, orbiting each other every 39.7 years, circles the bright pair every 2,084 years; their separation shrank from 10.7 arcseconds in 1841 to 4.5 in 1971. The system may be dynamically unstable and break apart within about 100,000 years.

sections.title: Dnoces
sections.text: Apollo astronauts nicknamed it Dnoces, “Second” spelled backwards, in honor of Apollo 1 astronaut Edward H. White II. The name was coined in 1967 by the Apollo 9 crew and Clarence Cleminshaw.

hip-56561.name: Lambda Centauri
hip-56561.introduction: is a blue-white giant in Centaurus, about 390 light-years away, near the nebula IC 2944.

sections.title: A flattened young star
sections.text: Spinning at about 183 km/s, it bulges 17% at the equator. It belongs to the Lower Centaurus–Crux group of the Scorpius–Centaurus association, 16 to 20 million years old.

hip-92041.name: Phi Sagittarii
hip-92041.introduction: is a blue-white star in the Teapot of Sagittarius, about 239 light-years away. Its proper name is Nandou.

sections.title: A binary confirmed at last
sections.text: It was catalogued as a spectroscopic binary, and a companion reported from a lunar occultation turned out to be spurious. Interferometry in 2017 finally confirmed a companion about 60% more massive than the Sun, orbiting roughly once a year about 1.3 AU away.

hip-45860.name: Alpha Lyncis
hip-45860.introduction: is the brightest star in Lynx, a red giant about 220 light-years away.

sections.title: Becoming a Mira?
sections.text: It has expanded to about 58 times the Sun’s radius. Its small, irregular variations suggest an inert carbon core wrapped in a helium-burning shell, a sign that it is starting to evolve into a Mira variable.

hip-31685.name: Pipit
hip-31685.introduction: is Nu Puppis, a blue-white Be shell star about 370 light-years away. Its name comes from the Kendayan people of West Kalimantan, after a bird known as the “rice thief.”

sections.title: A former south pole star
sections.text: Nu Puppis lies within a degree of the circle traced by the south celestial pole. From around 13,300 BCE it was the south pole star, with the pole passing closest about 12,330 BCE.

sections.title: Spinning edge-on
sections.text: Spinning at about 225 km/s, it is 17% wider at the equator, where it is about 3,000 K cooler than at its poles. We see its disk of gas edge-on.

orb6-17088+6543-a-b.name: Aldhibah
orb6-17088+6543-a-b.introduction: is Zeta Draconis, a blue-white giant about 330 light-years away. Its name, from the Arabic for “the wolf” or “hyena,” pairs it with Athebyne.

sections.title: Jupiter’s pole star
sections.text: Zeta Draconis is the north pole star of Jupiter. Earth’s north ecliptic pole lies roughly midway between it and Delta Draconis.

sections.title: A bright giant
sections.text: About six times larger and more massive than the Sun, it radiates 880 times the Sun’s light from a surface of about 13,400 K.

hip-23685.name: Epsilon Leporis
hip-23685.introduction: is an orange giant in Lepus, about 213 light-years away, 40 times the Sun’s radius.

sections.title: Ripples in a giant
sections.text: Its outer layers oscillate, showing velocity changes over a few days on top of a long-term trend, probably solar-like and Mira-like oscillations rather than rotation.

hip-84380.name: Pi Herculis
hip-84380.introduction: is the northeastern corner of the Keystone in Hercules, an orange bright giant about 367 light-years away.

sections.title: A pulse or a companion?
sections.text: With 4.5 times the Sun’s mass and about 60 times its radius, it varies by about 0.005 magnitudes over a day. A brown dwarf companion has been proposed, but weak pulsation of its atmosphere is the more likely cause. A planet would need to orbit 37 AU out, between Neptune’s and Pluto’s distances, to receive Earth-like warmth.

hip-46853.name: Theta Ursae Majoris
hip-46853.introduction: is a yellow-white star in Ursa Major, about 44 light-years away, with 1.4 times the Sun’s mass and nearly eight times its luminosity.

sections.title: A companion in question
sections.text: A 371-day spectroscopic orbit reported in 1976 was later questioned, and observations in 2009 found velocity changes without a clear orbit. A 14th-magnitude star 4.1 arcseconds away shares its motion. In Chinese tradition, it is the star of Shao Siming, a god of destiny.

cns5-gj-560.name: Xami
cns5-gj-560.introduction: is Alpha Circini, the brightest star in Circinus, about 54 light-years away. Its name refers to the South African “Eyes of the Lion,” Alpha and Beta Centauri, whose lion’s face covers this star.

sections.title: A six-minute pulse
sections.text: Alpha Circini pulsates in several patterns at once, the strongest repeating every 6.8 minutes, and its atmosphere is enriched with strontium, chromium and europium. It rotates every 4.5 days and has an orange dwarf companion. It may belong to the young Beta Pictoris moving group.

hip-75141.name: Delta Lupi
hip-75141.introduction: is a blue-white subgiant in Lupus, about 900 light-years away, with nearly 12 times the Sun’s mass.

sections.title: A massive pulsator
sections.text: About 15 million years old, it is a Beta Cephei variable pulsating six times a day and belongs to the Upper Centaurus–Lupus association.

hip-22449.name: Tabit
hip-22449.introduction: is Pi³ Orionis, the brightest star in the lion’s hide that Orion holds up as a shield, only about 26 light-years away. Its name comes from the Arabic for “the enduring,” or “fixed one.”

sections.title: A Sun-like neighbor
sections.text: Tabit is a yellow-white main-sequence star with about 1.3 times the Sun’s mass and 2.8 times its luminosity; since 1943 it has served as a classification standard. A 73-day velocity signal probably comes from stellar activity, and searches have excluded giant planets out to 5 AU, leaving room for planets in its habitable zone.

hip-83000.name: Kappa Ophiuchi
hip-83000.introduction: is an orange giant in Ophiuchus, about 92 light-years away.

sections.title: A red clump giant
sections.text: With 19% more mass than the Sun, it has expanded to about 11 times the Sun’s radius and now fuses helium in its core. It has been a spectral standard since 1943. Its listing as a variable may come from a mix-up with the nearby variable Chi Ophiuchi.

msc-21129+3014.name: Zeta Cygni
msc-21129+3014.introduction: is a yellow giant in Cygnus, about 143 light-years away, orbited by a hidden white dwarf every 17.8 years.

sections.title: Polluted by its partner
sections.text: Zeta Cygni A is a mild barium star: its atmosphere is enriched with heavy elements made by its companion when that star was an asymptotic-giant-branch star, then blown off and captured. Before receiving this material, the giant had about 2.5 solar masses, while its companion, now a white dwarf, had three.

hip-73714.name: Brachium
hip-73714.introduction: is Sigma Librae, a red giant about 260 light-years away. Its Latin name means “arm.”

sections.title: Once Gamma Scorpii
sections.text: It was designated Gamma Scorpii until 1930, when the IAU reassigned it to Libra. It was also the brightest star of the obsolete constellation Turdus Solitarius.

sections.title: Pulses within pulses
sections.text: An asymptotic-giant-branch star, it pulsates over about 20 days, with small changes as brief as 15 to 20 minutes. A faint companion more than 100,000 AU away may be bound to it.

msc-20113-0049.name: Antinous
msc-20113-0049.introduction: is Theta Aquilae, a pair of blue-white stars about 286 light-years away. Its name recalls the obsolete constellation Antinous, of which it was part.

sections.title: A close, eccentric pair
sections.text: The two stars orbit every 17.1 days on an eccentric path about 0.25 AU apart. The companion is a weak Am star with extra zirconium and barium in its atmosphere.

hip-32607.name: Alpha Pictoris
hip-32607.introduction: is the brightest star in Pictor, about 97 light-years away, and the south pole star of the planet Mercury.

sections.title: A shell star
sections.text: Spinning at about 206 km/s, it is surrounded by a shell of gas that it may have thrown off recently. It is one of the brightest known Delta Scuti variables and, unusually for an A-type star, emits X-rays, perhaps from its companion, which orbits about every three years and seven months.

msc-21287+7034.name: Alfirk
msc-21287+7034.introduction: is Beta Cephei, a triple star about 690 light-years away and the prototype of the Beta Cephei class of pulsating stars. Its name comes from the Arabic for “the flock.”

sections.title: A pulsating prototype
sections.text: Its brightness varies between magnitudes 3.16 and 3.27 every 0.19 days, about 4.6 hours. The primary is a hot blue subgiant with 7 to 12 times the Sun’s mass and only a few million years old.

hip-79882.name: Yed Posterior
hip-79882.introduction: is Epsilon Ophiuchi, a red giant about 106 light-years away; with Yed Prior it forms the hand of Ophiuchus. Its name comes from the Arabic for “hand,” and “posterior” because it follows Delta across the sky.

sections.title: A giant with an unusual recipe
sections.text: With nearly twice the Sun’s mass and an age of about a billion years, it is unusually poor in cyanogen and carbon for its class. Its solar-type oscillations allow asteroseismology, although models cannot yet tell whether it fuses hydrogen in a shell or helium in its core.

msc-07292-4318.name: Hadir
msc-07292-4318.introduction: is Sigma Puppis, an orange giant about 192 light-years away with a white companion visible in a telescope.

sections.title: A giant with shallow eclipses
sections.text: The giant has an unseen partner on a 257.8-day orbit, and the pair shows shallow eclipses. A third star 22 arcseconds away shares its motion. Olin Eggen named a moving group after it in 1970, although its existence has since been questioned.

hip-93194.name: Sulafat
hip-93194.introduction: is Gamma Lyrae, a blue-white giant about 620 light-years away. Its name comes from the Arabic for “turtle”: fine harps, like the lyre of Lyra, were made of tortoiseshell.

sections.title: Single after all
sections.text: About 15 times the Sun’s radius, it was long thought to be a spectroscopic binary but is now believed to be a single, rapidly rotating star.

hip-89962.name: Eta Serpentis
hip-89962.introduction: is the brightest star in Serpens Cauda, the serpent’s tail, about 60.5 light-years away.

sections.title: Not a carbon star
sections.text: It was once classified as a carbon star, which would have made it the brightest in the sky, but that classification proved wrong. It is an orange star between the subgiant and giant stages, showing solar-like oscillations. The star Gliese 710 currently lies just 1.6 light-years from it.

hip-17678.name: Gamma Hydri
hip-17678.introduction: is a red giant in Hydrus, about 214 light-years away.

sections.title: An expanded old star
sections.text: With about the Sun’s mass, it has expanded to 62 times the Sun’s radius and is most likely on the asymptotic giant branch. It varies slightly, between magnitudes 3.26 and 3.33.

orb6-04340-5503-a-b.name: Alpha Doradus
orb6-04340-5503-a-b.introduction: is the brightest star in Dorado, a binary about 169 light-years away.

sections.title: A giant and a subgiant
sections.text: A silicon-rich giant and a hotter subgiant orbit each other every 12 years, their separation swinging from 2 to 17.5 AU.

hip-113136.name: Skat
hip-113136.introduction: is Delta Aquarii, a white star about 113 light-years away. Its name comes from the Arabic for “shin.”

sections.title: A companion found in 2017
sections.text: With three times the Sun’s mass, it is probably a member of the 500-million-year-old Ursa Major moving group. Hipparcos data suggested a companion on a 483-day orbit, and infrared interferometry found one in 2017: probably a Sun-like star about 2 AU away.

msc-00393+3052.name: Delta Andromedae
msc-00393+3052.introduction: is an orange giant in Andromeda, about 106 light-years away. Its proper name, Kuda, is the Malay word for horse.

sections.title: A triple with a debris disk
sections.text: The giant has a faint K-dwarf companion about 11.6 AU away, imaged with a coronagraph, and a red dwarf at least 940 AU out. A debris disk surrounds the system.

msc-06149+2230.name: Propus
msc-06149+2230.introduction: is Eta Geminorum, a red giant in Gemini about 380 light-years away; Propus is Greek for “forward foot.”

sections.title: Eclipses every eight years
sections.text: Besides semiregular pulsations of about 234 days, it is eclipsed roughly every eight years by an unseen companion; the eclipses of 1980, 1988 and 2012 were well observed, each lasting several weeks. A visual companion, discovered by Burnham in 1881, orbits every 474 years.

sections.title: Near a supernova remnant
sections.text: It lies just west of the supernova remnant IC 443 and, 0.9 degrees from the ecliptic, can be occulted by the Moon; Venus last covered it in 1910.

hip-24305.name: Mu Leporis
hip-24305.introduction: is a blue-white star in Lepus, about 170 light-years away, with an atmosphere rich in mercury and manganese.

sections.title: A patchy surface and a hidden neighbor
sections.text: It may vary every 2.9 days as patches on its surface rotate into view. X-rays from a point about 52 AU away hint at a small companion.

hip-75458.name: Edasich
hip-75458.introduction: is Iota Draconis, an orange giant about 101 light-years away with two known substellar companions.

sections.title: Hypatia
sections.text: Its planet, found in 2002, was named Hypatia in 2015 after the ancient Greek astronomer and mathematician, a name proposed by a student society in Madrid. A second, more distant planet or brown dwarf was found in 2021, and astrometry measured the true masses of both.

sections.title: An orange-red star of old
sections.text: Edasich is the faintest star whose color was reported before the telescope: it was described as orange-red.

orb6-01061-4643-a-b.name: Beta Phoenicis
orb6-01061-4643-a-b.introduction: is a pair of yellow giants in Phoenix, about 182 light-years away.

sections.title: Twins that confuse the measurements
sections.text: The two similar G-type giants orbit every 171 years, less than an arcsecond apart. Their nearly equal brightness has made measuring their distance difficult.

hip-93864.name: Tau Sagittarii
hip-93864.introduction: is an orange giant in Sagittarius, part of the Teapot, about 122 light-years away.

sections.title: A visitor from elsewhere
sections.text: Its low metal content and a speed four times the local average suggest that it came from another part of the Galaxy. It is a red clump giant with about 1.25 solar masses, now fusing helium in its core.

hip-59774.name: Megrez
hip-59774.introduction: is Delta Ursae Majoris, the faintest of the seven Big Dipper stars, about 80 light-years away, where the bear’s tail meets its body. Its name comes from the Arabic for “the base of the tail.”

sections.title: A dusty, spinning star
sections.text: Megrez rotates rapidly, which flattens it and makes its poles hotter than its equator. A debris disk orbits about 16 AU out, unusually close for its age, perhaps because drag makes the dust spiral inward. It belongs to the Ursa Major moving group. Hindu tradition knew it as Atri, one of the Seven Rishis.

hip-50099.name: Omega Carinae
hip-50099.introduction: is the most southerly bright star of Carina and part of the Diamond Cross, about 342 light-years away.

sections.title: A future south pole star
sections.text: Omega Carinae is a blue-white shell star with a disk of gas around its equator, spinning at least 240 km/s against a breakup speed of about 320 km/s. Earth’s precession will bring the south celestial pole close to it around AD 5800.

cns5-gj-657.name: Eta Scorpii
cns5-gj-657.introduction: is a binary about 73 light-years away and the southernmost star of Scorpius with a Bayer letter.

sections.title: A fast spinner and a red dwarf
sections.text: The primary is a yellow-white subgiant with 1.6 times the Sun’s mass, about 1.1 billion years old, spinning so fast that it turns in less than a day. It emits X-rays and shows extra barium. Its companion, L 413-148, is a red dwarf with about half the Sun’s mass, shining at only magnitude 11.2.

hip-85267.name: Gamma Arae
hip-85267.introduction: is a blue supergiant in Ara, about 1,100 light-years away, radiating some 120,000 times as much energy as the Sun.

sections.title: A rapidly spinning supergiant
sections.text: Only about 16 million years old, it spins at about 269 km/s, completing a rotation roughly every 4.8 days, and its wind flows out mostly along the equator. Its motion traces back to the Scorpius region of the Milky Way, 20 to 25 degrees away.

hip-54879.name: Chertan
hip-54879.introduction: is Theta Leonis, a white star on the lion’s hip, about 165 light-years away. Its name comes from the Arabic for “two small ribs,” and its Latin name, Coxa, means “hip.”

sections.title: A dusty Am star
sections.text: About 550 million years old, it is a chemically peculiar Am star with strong metal lines, rapidly rotating but seen nearly pole-on. Excess infrared light points to a dust disk about 36 AU from the star.

hip-50371.name: q Carinae
hip-50371.introduction: is V337 Carinae, an orange bright giant in Carina that varies irregularly between magnitudes 3.36 and 3.44.

sections.title: A supernova candidate
sections.text: Benjamin Gould listed it as possibly variable in 1879; it was named V337 Carinae in 1973. With about nine times the Sun’s mass, it is considered a supernova candidate.

hip-109492.name: Zeta Cephei
hip-109492.introduction: is a red supergiant marking the left shoulder of Cepheus, roughly 840 to 1,000 light-years away, about 172 times the Sun’s size.

sections.title: A neutrino early warning?
sections.text: With about 10 times the Sun’s mass, it may end in a core-collapse supernova and was listed as a likely pre-supernova candidate in 2022. Detectors could catch its neutrinos hours before the collapse. It is also one of the fundamental standards of the MK spectral system, defining type K1.5 Ib.

hip-95501.name: Delta Aquilae
hip-95501.introduction: is a binary in Aquila, about 51 light-years away. Its proper name is Guqi. It is approaching the Sun and should pass within about 25 light-years in some 335,000 years.

sections.title: A pulsating subgiant with a hidden partner
sections.text: The primary is a yellow-white subgiant and a Delta Scuti variable, spinning at about 87 km/s. An unseen companion with about two-thirds of the Sun’s mass, probably a K-type star, tugs it around every 3.4 years.

hip-32362.name: Alzirr
hip-32362.introduction: is Xi Geminorum, a yellow-white subgiant at one of the twins’ feet, about 59 light-years away. Its name comes from the Arabic for “the button.”

sections.title: Perhaps two stars
sections.text: Usually treated as a single star with about 1.6 times the Sun’s mass, it may actually be a spectroscopic binary of two equal stars. It spins at about 66 km/s and emits X-rays.

hip-19780.name: Rhombus
hip-19780.introduction: is Alpha Reticuli, the brightest star in Reticulum, about 160 light-years away, a yellow giant best seen from the southern hemisphere.

sections.title: A probable wide partner
sections.text: It has expanded to 13 times the Sun’s radius. A 12th-magnitude star 48 arcseconds away shares its motion; with a 94% chance of being related, it would be about 2,400 AU away and take at least 60,000 years to orbit.

hip-8886.name: Segin
hip-8886.introduction: is Epsilon Cassiopeiae, a blue-white star in Cassiopeia’s W, about 430 to 460 light-years away. Its name probably comes from a miscopying of Seginus.

sections.title: A hot star with a shell
sections.text: With nine times the Sun’s mass and 3,000 times its luminosity, it shows signs of a shell of gas it has thrown off, like a Be star. It probably belongs to the Cas–Tau group, which may have been pulled away from the Alpha Persei Cluster. Some sources wrongly claim that it is Navi, the Apollo navigation star; that is Gamma Cassiopeiae.

hip-63090.name: Minelauva
hip-63090.introduction: is Delta Virginis, a red giant about 200 light-years away. Its name comes from the Arabic for “in the lunar mansion of ʽawwāʼ,” the Barker.

sections.title: A pulsating giant on the move
sections.text: With only 1.2 times the Sun’s mass, it has swollen to 67 times the Sun’s radius and shines nearly 700 times as brightly. It pulsates with several periods from 13 to 126 days and moves fast relative to its neighbors. An 11th-magnitude dwarf 80 arcseconds away may be a companion.

msc-08468+0625.name: Ashlesha
msc-08468+0625.introduction: is Epsilon Hydrae, a multiple star of at least four members about 129 light-years away, in the head of Hydra. Its name comes from the Sanskrit nakshatra Āślēṣā, “the embrace.”

sections.title: A family of stars
sections.text: A yellow giant, A, and its companion, B, form the central pair. A spectroscopic binary, C, with a 9.9-day orbit circles them every 870 years, 3 arcseconds away, and a fourth star, D, probably bound too, takes about 10,000 years.

hip-66249.name: Heze
hip-66249.introduction: is Zeta Virginis, a white star about 74 light-years away, just half a degree south of the celestial equator.

sections.title: A pulsator with a red-dwarf partner
