sections.text: With twice the Sun’s mass and radius, about half a billion years old, it is a Delta Scuti variable; students confirmed its variability while mining survey data. A red dwarf companion, found in 2010, orbits at least 25 AU away and probably explains the system’s X-rays.

hip-67464.name: Heng
hip-67464.introduction: is Nu Centauri, a hot binary about 440 light-years away in the Upper Centaurus–Lupus association.

sections.title: A partner that turns it into a Be star
sections.text: An unseen companion orbits every 2.6 days, and their interaction appears to produce the emission lines that make the primary a Be star. The primary has 8.5 times the Sun’s mass and is a Beta Cephei variable that is also stretched by tides.

hip-14354.name: Gorgonea Tertia
hip-14354.introduction: is Rho Persei, a red giant about 308 light-years away and the third of the four Gorgonea, named for the Gorgons in the legend of Perseus.

sections.title: A pulsating giant
sections.text: Johann Schmidt discovered in 1854 that it varies, between magnitudes 3.3 and 4.0 over periods of 50, 120 and 250 days. On the asymptotic giant branch, it has swollen to 143 times the Sun’s radius.

msc-09110-5858.name: a Carinae
msc-09110-5858.introduction: is V357 Carinae, a triple star about 419 light-years away near Aspidiske, in the heart of the False Cross.

sections.title: A very shallow eclipse
sections.text: Sergei Gaposchkin announced its variability in 1959. Its light dips by about 0.03 magnitudes every 6.74 days, the orbit of a very shallow eclipsing binary. Its motion also reveals an unseen third companion.

hip-102395.name: Beta Pavonis
hip-102395.introduction: is a white star in Pavo, about 135 light-years away, and a member of the Ursa Major moving group.

sections.title: An evolving star
sections.text: About 305 million years old, with 2.5 times the Sun’s mass, it is leaving the main sequence and still spins at about 75 km/s.

hip-112029.name: Homam
hip-112029.introduction: is Zeta Pegasi, a blue-white star about 204 light-years away. Its name means “man of high spirit.”

sections.title: Discovered variable by Gravity Probe B
sections.text: In 2007, data from the Gravity Probe B spacecraft showed that it is a slowly pulsating B star, varying slightly about once a day. It is about 120 million years old and spins at 140 to 210 km/s.

orb6-04287+1552-aa-ab.name: Chamukuy
orb6-04287+1552-aa-ab.introduction: is Theta² Tauri, the brighter star of the naked-eye pair Theta Tauri in the Hyades, about 157 light-years away. Its name means a small bird in Yucatec Maya.

sections.title: A pulsating giant and its partner
sections.text: Chamukuy is a white giant and a Delta Scuti variable that pulses every 1.8 hours. A sixth-magnitude companion orbits it every 141 days. Its naked-eye neighbor, Theta¹ Tauri, is an orange giant 5.6 arcminutes away, about 152 light-years from us.

hip-74395.name: Zeta Lupi
hip-74395.introduction: is a yellow giant in Lupus, about 117 light-years away, with a probable companion 71 arcseconds away.

sections.title: A helium-burning giant
sections.text: A red clump giant, it fuses helium in its core, with 2.6 times the Sun’s mass and nine times its size.

msc-16001-3824.name: Eta Lupi
msc-16001-3824.introduction: is a triple star in Lupus, about 440 light-years away, in the Upper Centaurus–Lupus association.

sections.title: Orbits of immense length
sections.text: A hot subgiant and a chemically peculiar A star, 15 arcseconds apart, take an estimated 27,000 years per orbit. A third, Sun-like star circles them about half a million years.

hip-49583.name: Eta Leonis
hip-49583.introduction: is a blue supergiant in Leo, about 1,270 light-years away. It appears faint, yet it is nearly 20,000 times as luminous as the Sun.

sections.title: A blue loop
sections.text: It is believed to be in a blue loop phase of its evolution and has served as a classification standard since 1943. It may be a multiple star, although its companions are uncertain.

msc-04007+1229.name: Lambda Tauri
msc-04007+1229.introduction: is a triple star in Taurus, about 480 light-years away, and only the third eclipsing binary ever discovered, in 1848.

sections.title: Eclipses and a third star
sections.text: Two stars about 0.1 AU apart eclipse each other, dimming the system from magnitude 3.37 to 3.91. A third star orbits them every 33 days, perturbing their orbit. In 1909, Lambda Tauri and Delta Librae were the first stars in which Frank Schlesinger saw spectral lines broadened by rotation.

hip-50335.name: Adhafera
hip-50335.introduction: is Zeta Leonis, the second star of the Sickle in Leo’s mane, about 274 light-years away. Its name comes from the Arabic for “the lock of hair,” a name originally given to Coma Berenices.

sections.title: A giant and a false partner
sections.text: With three times the Sun’s mass and 10.5 times its radius, it shines 220 times as brightly and has served as a classification standard since 1943. Its apparent companion, 35 Leonis, is only about 100 light-years away and unrelated.

hip-6867.name: Gamma Phoenicis
hip-6867.introduction: is a red giant in Phoenix, about 234 light-years away, with an unseen companion.

sections.title: A giant distorted by its partner
sections.text: The two stars orbit every 194 days. The changing light is probably due to the giant’s distorted shape as it orbits rather than eclipses. Signs of hot coronal activity may come from the companion pulling material from the giant.

msc-18501+3322.name: Sheliak
msc-18501+3322.introduction: is Beta Lyrae, about 960 light-years away: a close eclipsing binary whose stars exchange mass.

sections.title: A star feeding its partner
sections.text: The fainter star was once the more massive; as it swelled into a giant, it poured most of its mass onto its companion. The companion, now the heavier star, is hidden in a thick disk with jet-like features. Mass flows at about one solar mass every 50,000 years, lengthening the orbit by about 19 seconds each year.

cns5-gj-78.1.name: Mothallah
cns5-gj-78.1.introduction: is Alpha Trianguli, a binary about 63 light-years away at the head of the triangle; its name comes from the Arabic for “the head of the triangle.”

sections.title: A star stretched by its partner
sections.text: The yellow-white primary and its companion orbit every 1.7 days. The fast-spinning primary is distorted into an egg shape, so the light varies as it orbits. In a few million years, as the primary grows into a red giant, it may begin passing mass to its companion. A red dwarf 36 arcminutes away, found in 2018 to share its motion, makes the system triple.

sections.title: The wolf of Babylon
sections.text: In the Babylonian compendium MUL.APIN, it is UR.BAR.RA, “the wolf,” called “the seeder of the plough.” With Beta Trianguli, Arab astronomers called it the Scale Beam.

hip-41704.name: Muscida
hip-41704.introduction: is Omicron Ursae Majoris, a yellow giant at the bear’s snout, about 179 light-years away. Its name comes from Latin for “snout.”

sections.title: A runaway with a planet
sections.text: In 2012, a gas giant about 4.1 times Jupiter’s mass was found on a 1,630-day orbit. Muscida moves at about 35 km/s relative to nearby stars, enough to count as a runaway. A faint companion 7 arcseconds away is probably the source of the system’s X-rays.

hip-93805.name: Lambda Aquilae
hip-93805.introduction: is a blue-white star in Aquila, about 127 light-years away, one of the steadiest stars Hipparcos measured. Its name comes from the Arabic for “the two ostriches.”

sections.title: A red-dwarf partner found by the VLT
sections.text: Interferometry at the Very Large Telescope resolved a red dwarf companion orbiting about every 15 days. The companion explains the X-rays coming from this young star system, about 90 million years old. In about 300 million years, the primary’s growth into a red giant should start a mass transfer between them.

msc-13496-4228.name: Mu Centauri
msc-13496-4228.introduction: is a hot Be star in Centaurus, about 510 light-years away, and a spectral standard for its type.

sections.title: A star with outbursts
sections.text: It spins once every 11.6 hours, so its poles reach about 23,000 K while its equator is near 17,600 K. Outbursts feed its disk of gas, and its brightness varies between magnitudes 2.92 and 3.49. It belongs to the Upper Centaurus–Lupus association.

hip-50372.name: Tania Borealis
hip-50372.introduction: is Lambda Ursae Majoris, a white subgiant about 138 light-years away. Its name combines the Arabic for “the second spring of the gazelle” with the Latin borealis, “northern.”

sections.title: Leaving the main sequence
sections.text: After 410 million years, with 2.4 times the Sun’s mass, it is beginning to evolve into a giant.

hip-48774.name: Phi Velorum
hip-48774.introduction: is a blue-white supergiant in Vela, about 1,590 light-years away, radiating about 28,000 times the Sun’s luminosity.

sections.title: A supergiant
sections.text: It has exhausted its core hydrogen and left the main sequence. It has about 10 times the Sun’s mass and 31 times its radius.

hip-5364.name: Eta Ceti
hip-5364.introduction: is an orange giant in Cetus, about 121 light-years away, with two giant planets. Its proper name, Gajahmina, comes from a Balinese constellation, an “elephant-fish” matching Cetus.

sections.title: Two planets in resonance
sections.text: Its planets have at least 2.6 and 3.3 Jupiter masses and orbits of 404 and 752 days. If their orbits share a plane, they must be locked in a 2:1 resonance; otherwise the system would be unstable.

hip-90422.name: Alpha Telescopii
hip-90422.introduction: is the brightest star in Telescopium, about 278 light-years away. Ptolemy placed it in Corona Australis, but Lacaille moved it to Telescopium when he created that constellation in the 18th century.

sections.title: A magnetic subgiant
sections.text: Radiating nearly 800 times the Sun’s luminosity, it has a magnetic field of about 230 gauss. Its slow apparent rotation suggests we see it nearly pole-on.

hip-112623.name: Epsilon Gruis
hip-112623.introduction: is a white subgiant in Grus, about 129 light-years away.

sections.title: A flattened, dusty star
sections.text: About 249 million years old, it spins at about 235 km/s, bulging 18% at the equator. Excess infrared light suggests a dust disk, and a suspected active companion probably produces its weak X-rays.

msc-19588+1930.name: Gamma Sagittae
msc-19588+1930.introduction: is the brightest star in Sagitta, a red giant about 288 light-years away. Its proper name, Telum, is Latin for “dart.”

sections.title: A historic name
sections.text: Telum was a historic name for the whole constellation: it labels Sagitta on the first printed star map, by Albrecht Dürer in 1515. The star itself is a red giant about 2.4 billion years old, 58 times the Sun’s radius.

hip-33856.name: Nganurganity
hip-33856.introduction: is Sigma Canis Majoris, a red supergiant about 1,290 light-years away. To the Boorong people of Victoria, it is the Jacky lizard, an ancestral figure who fights the Moon, flanked by his wives, Delta and Epsilon Canis Majoris.

sections.title: A swollen supergiant
sections.text: It has ballooned to 290 times the Sun’s radius, wider than Earth’s orbit, and radiates more than 15,800 times the Sun’s light. It is a potential supernova progenitor whose neutrinos could give early warning of its collapse.

msc-02433+0314.name: Kaffaljidhma
msc-02433+0314.introduction: is Gamma Ceti, a triple star about 80 light-years away. Its name comes from the Arabic for “the cut-short hand.”

sections.title: A colorful challenge
sections.text: A white main-sequence star and a fainter yellow-white companion, 2.6 arcseconds apart, make a popular target for amateur telescopes because of their contrasting colors, though they can be hard to split. A third, orange dwarf shares their motion more than 20,000 AU away.

hip-112748.name: Sadalbari
hip-112748.introduction: is Mu Pegasi, a yellow giant about 113 light-years away, visible even on a moonlit night.

sections.title: A young giant
sections.text: About 520 million years old, with 2.6 times the Sun’s mass, it has expanded to nine times the Sun’s radius.

orb6-15155+3319-a-b.name: Delta Boötis
orb6-15155+3319-a-b.introduction: is a yellow giant in Boötes, about 120 light-years away, with a Sun-like companion visible in binoculars or a small telescope.

sections.title: A slow partnership
sections.text: The giant and its companion are at least 3,800 AU apart; if bound, they take at least 120,000 years per orbit. The star is sometimes called Princeps, Latin for “prince.”

hip-81833.name: Eta Herculis
hip-81833.introduction: is a yellow giant in the Keystone of Hercules, about 110 light-years away.

sections.title: A guide to M13
sections.text: Following the line from Eta to Zeta Herculis leads to M13, one of the finest globular clusters in the night sky, discovered by Edmond Halley in 1714. Eta Herculis has about twice the Sun’s mass and 9.3 times its radius.

hip-93085.name: Xi² Sagittarii
hip-93085.introduction: is a yellow-orange giant in Sagittarius, about 390 light-years away. Its proper name is Jian.

sections.title: A giant with a hidden partner
sections.text: With 3.6 times the Sun’s mass, about 380 million years old, it has grown to 27 times the Sun’s radius. Hipparcos data suggest an unseen companion.

msc-17376-1524.name: Xi Serpentis
msc-17376-1524.introduction: is a triple star in Serpens Cauda, about 105 light-years away. It is approaching and will pass about 27 light-years from the Sun in some 690,000 years.

sections.title: A peculiar giant and a tiny partner
sections.text: The primary, a chemically peculiar star rich in strontium, has twice the Sun’s mass; a companion with only 18% of the Sun’s mass orbits it every 2.3 days. A third star 24 arcseconds away takes an estimated 14,800 years per orbit.

hip-73555.name: Nekkar
hip-73555.introduction: is Beta Boötis, a yellow giant marking the herdsman’s head, about 235 light-years away. Its name comes from the Arabic for “the herdsman.”

sections.title: A surprising X-ray flare
sections.text: In 1993, the ROSAT satellite recorded an X-ray flare from Nekkar, the first such observation for a low-activity star of this type. An unseen red dwarf companion could explain it, and its extra barium points to a white dwarf companion too.

hip-40526.name: Tarf
hip-40526.introduction: is Beta Cancri, the brightest star in Cancer, about 303 light-years away. Its name comes from the Arabic for “end” or “edge.”

sections.title: A barium giant with a planet
sections.text: A barium star with 1.7 times the Sun’s mass, it has expanded to 52 times the Sun’s radius. A planet of at least 7.8 Jupiter masses orbits it every 605 days. A faint red dwarf at least 2,740 AU away may be bound to it.

hip-27288.name: Zeta Leporis
hip-27288.introduction: is a white star in Lepus with the first asteroid belt discovered beyond the Solar System.

sections.title: A massive asteroid belt
sections.text: Dust within about 5.4 AU of the star, confirmed in 2001, is thought to come from an asteroid belt some 200 times as massive as our own, more than half the Moon’s mass. Because the dust should fall into the star within 20,000 years, collisions must keep replenishing it.

sections.title: Once the brightest star
sections.text: About a million years ago, Zeta Leporis passed about 5.3 light-years from the Sun and was the brightest star in the night sky, at magnitude −2.05.

orb6-15496-0326-a-b.name: Mu Serpentis
orb6-15496-0326-a-b.introduction: is a white star in Serpens Caput, about 170 light-years away, with a companion detected by interferometry.

sections.title: A 36-year orbit
sections.text: The two stars orbit each other about every 36 years. The primary is a white main-sequence star; the companion’s type is uncertain.

msc-07201+2159.name: Wasat
msc-07201+2159.introduction: is Delta Geminorum, a white star in Gemini. Its name comes from the Arabic for “middle.”

sections.title: Pluto’s discovery spot
sections.text: In 1930, Clyde Tombaugh discovered the dwarf planet Pluto about half a degree east of this star. Lying just 0.18 degrees from the ecliptic, Wasat can be occulted by the Moon and, rarely, by planets: Saturn covered it in 1857, and Venus will in 2420.

sections.title: An orange companion
sections.text: A small telescope shows a cooler, orange companion, which may take several centuries to orbit. The system is approaching and should pass within about 6.7 light-years of the Sun in 1.1 million years.

hip-20889.name: Ain
hip-20889.introduction: is Epsilon Tauri, an orange giant in the Hyades, about 146 light-years away. Its name comes from the Arabic for “eye,” and Flamsteed called it Oculus Boreus, the “northern eye.”

sections.title: The first planet in a cluster
sections.text: Its giant planet, Amateru, was the first planet discovered in an open cluster. Its name, chosen in 2015, comes from the Shinto Sun goddess Amaterasu, born from the left eye of the god Izanagi. As a Hyades member, the star’s age is well known: about 625 million years.

hip-56343.name: Xi Hydrae
hip-56343.introduction: is a yellow giant in Hydra, about 130 light-years away, once listed by Flamsteed as 19 Crateris.

sections.title: Listening to a giant
sections.text: It has just reached the foot of the red giant branch, about 510 million years old. Its solar-like oscillations, with periods of 2 to 5.5 hours, make it an important target for asteroseismology.

hip-17378.name: Rana
hip-17378.introduction: is Delta Eridani, a star about 30 light-years away that is nearly finished as a subgiant and about to become a giant. Its name, “the frog,” was probably borrowed by mistake from Diphda, the Arabic “second frog.”

sections.title: An old neighbor seen pole-on
sections.text: About six billion years old, with 33% more mass than the Sun, it has expanded to 2.35 times the Sun’s size. It is very quiet magnetically, and its slow apparent rotation suggests we see it nearly pole-on. An old suspicion that it has a companion was not confirmed.

hip-112724.name: Iota Cephei
hip-112724.introduction: is an orange giant in Cepheus, about 115 light-years away, fusing helium in its core.

sections.title: A future guide to the pole
sections.text: In about 3,000 years, Earth’s precession will make it one of the closest visible stars to the north celestial pole, together with Alfirk on the other side of the pole’s path.

hip-75177.name: Phi¹ Lupi
hip-75177.introduction: is an orange giant in Lupus, about 275 light-years away, 40 times the Sun’s radius and over 1,400 times as luminous.

sections.title: A faint flicker
sections.text: It varies by less than a hundredth of a magnitude over 4.8 days, for reasons not yet known.

orb6-22102+0612-a-b.name: Biham
orb6-22102+0612-a-b.introduction: is Theta Pegasi, a white star about 92 light-years away. Its name comes from an Arabic phrase meaning “lucky stars of the young beasts.”

sections.title: A red dwarf found in 2021
sections.text: A slight acceleration measured by Hipparcos hinted at a companion, and in 2021 a red dwarf was found orbiting about 6.6 AU away. The primary, about 448 million years old, spins at about 136 km/s.

orb6-09036+4709-a-b.name: Alkaphrah
orb6-09036+4709-a-b.introduction: is Kappa Ursae Majoris, a pair of white stars about 358 light-years away. With Talitha, it formed the third “leap of the gazelle” of Arabic tradition.

sections.title: Twins with a dusty disk
sections.text: The two stars, of magnitudes 4.2 and 4.5, orbit each other every 35.6 years, only 0.18 arcseconds apart. A debris disk circles the primary about 55 AU out.

hip-1562.name: Iota Ceti
hip-1562.introduction: is an orange giant in Cetus, about 279 light-years away, traditionally called Deneb Kaitos Shemali, “the northern tail of the sea monster.”

sections.title: A wide companion
sections.text: With 3.7 times the Sun’s mass and 30 times its radius, it may vary slightly. A 10th-magnitude star 106 arcseconds away shares its motion.

hip-35350.name: Lambda Geminorum
hip-35350.introduction: is a white star in Gemini, about 101 light-years away, possibly part of a trailing tidal tail of the Hyades stream.

sections.title: Companions and a hot inner disk
sections.text: E. B. Frost found it to be a spectroscopic binary in 1924, a companion confirmed during a lunar occultation; a fainter star 9.3 arcseconds away forms a wide pair. Infrared light reveals dust remarkably close to the star, within about 0.65 AU.

msc-04179-3348.name: Upsilon⁴ Eridani
msc-04179-3348.introduction: is a close pair of blue-white stars in Eridanus, about 178 light-years away.

sections.title: Near-identical twins
sections.text: The two B-type stars orbit every five days on a circular path, their spins synchronized with the orbit. Both show unusual amounts of mercury and manganese, and their properties are nearly identical.

hip-55282.name: Delta Crateris
hip-55282.introduction: is the brightest star in Crater, an orange giant about 192 light-years away, occasionally called Labrum.

sections.title: A slow-spinning giant
sections.text: About 2.9 billion years old, it fuses helium in its core and has expanded to 20 times the Sun’s radius; its rotation is too slow to measure.

hip-99240.name: Delta Pavonis
hip-99240.introduction: is a Sun-like star in Pavo, only about 20 light-years away, one of the nearest bright stars to the Solar System. It is approaching and will pass about 17.8 light-years from us in some 49,000 years.

sections.title: An older, richer Sun
sections.text: With 107% of the Sun’s mass, about 6.1 billion years old, it shines 24% brighter than the Sun. It has more than twice the Sun’s iron abundance, which makes planets more likely. A trend in its velocity, reported in 2023, may point to a planet with an orbit of at least 37 years.

msc-07444+2424.name: Kappa Geminorum
msc-07444+2424.introduction: is a yellow giant in Gemini, about 141 light-years away, with an 8th-magnitude companion 7.2 arcseconds away.

sections.title: A standard giant
sections.text: About two billion years old, with twice the Sun’s mass, it has expanded to 11 times the Sun’s radius. Since 1943 it has served as a classification standard. In Japanese, it is Takahiro-boshi, the “esteemed nobility star.”

hip-10602.name: Phi Eridani
hip-10602.introduction: is a blue-white star in Eridanus, about 154 light-years away, a member of the 45-million-year-old Tucana–Horologium association.

sections.title: A flattened young star
sections.text: Spinning at about 250 km/s, it bulges 17% at the equator. A Sun-like 9th-magnitude star 86 arcseconds away may be a wide companion.

hip-100064.name: Algedi
hip-100064.introduction: is Alpha² Capricorni, the brighter star of a naked-eye pair in Capricornus. Its name comes from the Arabic for “the kid,” a young goat.

sections.title: A double by chance
sections.text: Alpha¹ and Alpha² Capricorni appear only 0.11 degrees apart and can be split with the naked eye, like Mizar and Alcor, but they are physically unrelated.

hip-86929.name: Eta Pavonis
hip-86929.introduction: is an orange bright giant in Pavo, about 350 light-years away, between a giant and a supergiant in luminosity.

sections.title: An expanded star
sections.text: It has expanded to about 33.5 times the Sun’s radius and radiates 469 times the Sun’s light.

hip-71053.name: Rho Boötis
hip-71053.introduction: is an orange giant in Boötes, about 164 light-years away.

sections.title: An active giant
sections.text: With about 1.2 times the Sun’s mass, it has expanded to 20.6 times the Sun’s size and is an RS Canum Venaticorum variable. Since 1943 it has served as a classification standard. In Bali, Boötes is Kala Sungsang, the upside-down demon.

hip-6537.name: Theta Ceti
hip-6537.introduction: is an orange giant in Cetus, about 112 light-years away. Its proper name is Tiancang.

sections.title: A helium-burning giant
sections.text: With 1.8 times the Sun’s mass, it fuses helium in its core and has expanded to 10 times the Sun’s radius. With Eta, Tau, Zeta and Upsilon Ceti, it formed the Arabic Hen Ostriches.

hip-13209.name: Bharani
hip-13209.introduction: is 41 Arietis, a blue-white star about 166 light-years away. Its name is that of the second nakshatra, or lunar mansion, of Hindu astronomy.

sections.title: A lily, a fly and a ram
sections.text: Bode counted it in the asterism Musca Borealis, the northern fly, and Lacaille in the defunct constellation Lilium, the lily. It spins at about 175 km/s, bulging 12% at the equator, has a close companion, and may belong to the AB Doradus moving group.

orb6-09307-4028-a-b.name: Psi Velorum
orb6-09307-4028-a-b.introduction: is a pair of yellow-white stars in Vela, about 61 light-years away, a candidate member of the Castor moving group.

sections.title: A 34-year orbit
sections.text: The two stars orbit every 34.1 years about 0.8 arcseconds apart. The fainter one has been reported to vary.

gj-216.name: Gamma Leporis
gj-216.introduction: is a yellow-white star in Lepus, only about 29 light-years away, with a companion, AK Leporis, easy to see in binoculars.

sections.title: A target for finding Earths
sections.text: About 1.3 billion years old and slightly larger than the Sun, it was a high-priority target for NASA’s planned Terrestrial Planet Finder. AK Leporis, 95 arcseconds away, is a BY Draconis variable. Both belong to the Ursa Major moving group.

hip-33018.name: Theta Geminorum
hip-33018.introduction: is a white subgiant in Gemini, about 189 light-years away.

sections.title: A young, flattened star
sections.text: About 252 million years old, it spins at about 133 km/s, bulging 11% at the equator. Five faint visual companions lie within 100 arcseconds.

hip-15900.name: Omicron Tauri
hip-15900.introduction: is a yellow giant in Taurus, about 270 light-years away, with an unseen companion.

sections.title: A slow giant
sections.text: With three times the Sun’s mass and 18 to 20 times its radius, it rotates about once every 533 days. A companion of at least 0.57 solar masses orbits it every 4.5 years.

hip-49841.name: Lambda Hydrae
hip-49841.introduction: is an orange giant in Hydra, about 109 light-years away, fusing helium in its core.

sections.title: A galaxy next door
sections.text: The spiral galaxy NGC 3145 appears just 7.8 arcminutes away, far beyond the star.

orb6-01315+1521-a-b.name: Alpherg
orb6-01315+1521-a-b.introduction: is Eta Piscium, a yellow giant about 350 light-years away. Neo-Babylonian astronomers called it Kullat Nūnu, the cord or bucket binding the fish.

sections.title: An 850-year orbit
sections.text: S. W. Burnham discovered its companion in 1878; the pair orbit every 850 years or so. The giant has a weak magnetic field.

hip-85727.name: Delta Arae
hip-85727.introduction: is a pair of blue-white stars in Ara, about 198 light-years away.

sections.title: An edge-on, eccentric orbit
sections.text: The two stars orbit every 2.5 years on a very elongated path seen almost edge-on. The primary spins at about 255 km/s, bulging 13% at the equator.

msc-03492+2403.name: Atlas
msc-03492+2403.introduction: is 27 Tauri, a binary in the Pleiades, about 444 light-years away, named after the Titan who fathered the Pleiades sisters in Greek myth.

sections.title: A pair with a vanishing third
sections.text: Two stars orbit every 291 days without eclipses; the primary spins fast enough to be noticeably flattened. A third star was reported in 1929 but has never been seen again, even with modern instruments.

hip-42536.name: Omicron Velorum
hip-42536.introduction: is the brightest star of the open cluster IC 2391, the Omicron Velorum Cluster, about 495 light-years away.

sections.title: A slowly pulsating star
sections.text: Alan Cousins discovered in 1959 that it varies slightly over 2.8 days; it is a slowly pulsating B star.

msc-20375+1436.name: Rotanev
msc-20375+1436.introduction: is Beta Delphini, the brightest star in Delphinus, about 101 light-years away.

sections.title: A joke in the catalog
sections.text: The names Rotanev and Sualocin first appeared in the Palermo Star Catalogue of 1814. Decades later, Thomas Webb discovered that, spelled backwards, they give Nicolaus Venator, the Latinized name of Niccolò Cacciatore, Piazzi’s assistant: a practical joke that has endured.

sections.title: A tight pair
sections.text: Two yellow-white stars orbit every 26.7 years only 0.44 arcseconds apart, a challenge to split in a telescope.

hip-114341.name: Safina
hip-114341.introduction: is 88 Aquarii, an orange giant about 271 light-years away. It belonged to the Arabic constellation Safina, the Ship, between Diphda and Fomalhaut.

sections.title: A cool giant
sections.text: Interferometry gives a radius about 29 times the Sun’s.

hip-20205.name: Prima Hyadum
hip-20205.introduction: is Gamma Tauri, the “first of the Hyades,” an orange giant near the center of the nearest open cluster, about 154 light-years away.

sections.title: A giant in a young cluster
sections.text: It fuses helium in its core; the CHARA array measured its radius at 13.4 times the Sun’s. With 2.7 times the Sun’s mass, it takes about 253 days to rotate.

msc-22288-0001.name: Zeta Aquarii
msc-22288-0001.introduction: is a triple star at the center of the Water Jar of Aquarius, about 95 light-years away. It crossed the celestial equator into the northern sky in 2004.

sections.title: A hidden third star
sections.text: A telescope shows two yellow-white stars. In 1942 Kaj Strand noticed wobbles revealing a third star; claimed images in 1979 and 1982 proved spurious, and it was not imaged until 2009. It orbits the brighter star every 26 years.

msc-11456-6644.name: Lambda Muscae
msc-11456-6644.introduction: is the tail of the Fly, a white star about 128 light-years away.

sections.title: Two red-dwarf companions
sections.text: Two red dwarfs orbit the A-type primary, at about 1.65 and 6.4 AU.

hip-103227.name: Beta Indi
hip-103227.introduction: is an orange bright giant in Indus, about 600 light-years away, 56 times the Sun’s size.

sections.title: A hybrid giant
sections.text: Only 53 million years old, with 6.7 times the Sun’s mass, it has both a hot corona and a cool wind, a combination called a hybrid giant.

hip-88714.name: Theta Arae
hip-88714.introduction: is a blue-white supergiant in Ara, about 810 light-years away.

sections.title: A young supergiant
sections.text: About 28 million years old, with nearly nine times the Sun’s mass and over 20 times its radius, it spins at about 95 km/s.

spectroscopic-hip-26207.name: Meissa
spectroscopic-hip-26207.introduction: is Lambda Orionis, a double star in Orion about 1,300 light-years away: a hot O-type giant with about 34 times the Sun’s mass. Its name comes from the Arabic for “the shining one,” originally meant for Alhena.

sections.title: A star in a supernova ring
sections.text: Meissa lights up the H II region Sh2-264, surrounded by an expanding ring of cool gas a few million years old. A former partner that exploded as a supernova could explain both the ring and Meissa’s motion.

sections.title: Mostly invisible light
sections.text: Although more luminous than Rigel and only slightly farther away, it looks three magnitudes fainter, because most of its energy is ultraviolet. A blue-white companion lies 4.4 arcseconds away.

hip-77233.name: Chow
hip-77233.introduction: is Beta Serpentis, a white star about 155 light-years away and a member of the Ursa Major moving group.

sections.title: A flattened star
sections.text: Spinning at about 217 km/s, it is flattened: about 4.2 times the Sun’s radius at the equator but 3.1 at the poles, which are more than 2,000 K hotter. An orange dwarf 31 arcseconds away is a companion.

hip-106985.name: Nashira
hip-106985.introduction: is Gamma Capricorni, a white star about 171 light-years away. Its name comes from the Arabic for “the lucky one” or “bearer of good news.”

sections.title: A puzzling chemistry
sections.text: Its spectrum shows extra strontium, chromium and europium, but whether it is an Ap or Am star is still debated. Lying 2.6 degrees from the ecliptic, it can be occulted by the Moon.

cns5-gj-3559.name: 23 Ursae Majoris
cns5-gj-3559.introduction: is a yellow-white subgiant in Ursa Major, about 78 light-years away, with a 9th-magnitude companion 22.7 arcseconds away.

sections.title: An evolving star
sections.text: With 1.9 times the Sun’s mass and 2.9 times its radius, it shines 15 times as brightly.

msc-04512+0536.name: Pi⁴ Orionis
msc-04512+0536.introduction: is a hot B-type giant in western Orion, about 1,050 light-years away, with a close companion.

sections.title: A massive pair
sections.text: A companion orbits every 9.5 days. The primary has nearly 11 times the Sun’s mass, is about 15 million years old, and shows a strong lack of boron.

orb6-14044+6423-a-b.name: Thuban
orb6-14044+6423-a-b.introduction: is Alpha Draconis, the north pole star from the 4th to the 2nd millennium BC. Today it is an inconspicuous white star, but the inner Big Dipper stars Phecda and Megrez point toward it.

sections.title: The ancient pole star
sections.text: Thuban was closest to the pole in 2830 BC, less than 10 arcminutes away, and stayed the pole star until about 1800 BC, when Kochab took over. It will be the pole star again in 20,346 AD.

sections.title: An eclipsing pair
sections.text: Thuban is a binary with a 51.4-day orbit. The fainter star was resolved by interferometry, and TESS observations revealed eclipses.

hip-42828.name: Alpha Pyxidis
hip-42828.introduction: is the brightest star in Pyxis, a hot blue-white giant with more than ten times the Sun’s mass.

sections.title: A future supernova
sections.text: About 10,000 times as luminous as the Sun, it is a Beta Cephei variable. Stars this massive are expected to end their lives as supernovae.

orb6-15278+2906-a-b.name: Nusakan
orb6-15278+2906-a-b.introduction: is Beta Coronae Borealis, a binary about 112 light-years away. Its name comes from the Arabic for “the two lines” of stars.

sections.title: A rapid pulsator
sections.text: The brighter star is a rapidly oscillating Ap star, pulsing every 16.2 minutes. Speckle interferometry resolved the pair in 1973; they orbit every 10.5 years.

hip-77622.name: Epsilon Serpentis
hip-77622.introduction: is a white Am star in Serpens Caput, about 70 light-years away.

sections.title: A possible warm disk
sections.text: About half a billion years old, it may have a warm dust disk about 4.2 AU from the star.

hip-15474.name: Tau⁴ Eridani
hip-15474.introduction: is a red giant in Eridanus, about 300 light-years away, more than 100 times the Sun’s radius.

sections.title: A slowly varying giant
sections.text: On the asymptotic giant branch, it varies irregularly between magnitudes 3.57 and 3.72. A 9.5-magnitude companion lies 5.7 arcseconds away.

hip-87933.name: Xi Herculis
hip-87933.introduction: is a yellow giant in Hercules, about 137 light-years away, a suspected member of the Sirius stream.

sections.title: A gently varying giant
sections.text: Hipparcos data revealed that it varies by about 0.03 magnitudes over 121 days. It fuses helium in its core and is about 2.5 billion years old.

hip-114971.name: Gamma Piscium
hip-114971.introduction: is a yellow giant in the Circlet of Pisces, about 135 light-years away. Its proper name is Yunyu.

sections.title: A visitor with a planet
sections.text: With only a quarter of the Sun’s metal content and a fast speed, it seems to be a visitor from another part of the Milky Way. A gas giant planet was found in 2021.

hip-17499.name: Electra
hip-17499.introduction: is the third-brightest star of the Pleiades, about 440 light-years away, named after one of the Seven Sisters of Greek myth.

sections.title: A fast-spinning Be star
sections.text: Spinning at about 320 km/s at its equator, it is flattened and gravity-darkened. Material thrown off roughly every ten years settles into a gas disk. Claims of companions have never been confirmed.

hip-9007.name: Chi Eridani
hip-9007.introduction: is a yellow subgiant in Eridanus, about 58 light-years away, with a faint companion 5 arcseconds away.

sections.title: An unusually variable subgiant
sections.text: Unusually for its class, it varies by 0.04 magnitudes, perhaps because of past mass transfer from its companion or an undiscovered third star.

gj-771.name: Alshain
gj-771.introduction: is Beta Aquilae, a yellow subgiant about 44 light-years away beside Altair. Its name, like Tarazed’s, comes from the Persian for “the scale beam.”

sections.title: A quiet Sun’s cousin
sections.text: Its very low magnetic activity may resemble the Sun’s Maunder minimum. It has served as a classification standard since 1943. A red-dwarf companion 13 arcseconds away is itself a double. The system will pass within 27 light-years in about 207,000 years.

hip-28103.name: Eta Leporis
hip-28103.introduction: is a yellow-white star in Lepus, about 49 light-years away.

sections.title: A dusty neighbor
sections.text: Spitzer found excess infrared light that can be modeled as a dust disk extending from 1 to 16 AU.

hip-57399.name: Taiyangshou
hip-57399.introduction: is Chi Ursae Majoris, an orange giant about 198 light-years away. Its name comes from the Chinese for “the Sun governor.”

sections.title: A guide to a galaxy
sections.text: It fuses helium in its core and has expanded to 23 times the Sun’s radius. The spiral galaxy NGC 3877 lies just 15 arcminutes south.

hip-8645.name: Baten Kaitos
hip-8645.introduction: is Zeta Ceti, an orange giant about 253 light-years away. Its name comes from the Arabic for “belly of the sea monster.”

sections.title: A weak barium star
sections.text: It is a weak barium star with 2.3 times the Sun’s mass. Its apparent partner, HD 11366, is far behind it.

hip-107089.name: Nu Octantis
hip-107089.introduction: is the brightest star in Octans, about 74 light-years away, with a white dwarf companion and a planet.

sections.title: A planet in a binary
sections.text: The planet orbits the primary halfway between it and the white dwarf, which circles every 2.9 years, and may move on a retrograde orbit, opposite to the stars’ motion. A study in 2025 confirmed the planet. Because the stars were once closer, the planet probably did not form where it is now.

hip-72220.name: Maenalus
hip-72220.introduction: is 109 Virginis, a white star about 135 light-years away and the brightest star of the obsolete constellation Mons Maenalus, a mountain in Greece.

sections.title: A flattened star
sections.text: Spinning at about 285 km/s, it bulges an estimated 31% at the equator.

spectroscopic-hip-30867.name: Beta Monocerotis
spectroscopic-hip-30867.introduction: is the brightest star in Monoceros, about 700 light-years away: a curved line of three Be stars in a telescope. William Herschel, who discovered the triple in 1781, called it “one of the most beautiful sights in the heavens.”

sections.title: Three spinning stars
sections.text: All three components are Be stars, hot stars surrounded by disks of gas. They share the same motion and nearly the same velocities, so they are thought to lie at the same distance. The system varies slightly in brightness, though it is unclear which star is responsible.

hip-105881.name: Zeta Capricorni
hip-105881.introduction: is a yellow supergiant in Capricornus, about 386 light-years away, and a prototypical barium star.

sections.title: A gift from a dead companion
sections.text: Its atmosphere is enriched with barium, carbon and other elements made by its companion, now a white dwarf of about two-thirds of the Sun’s mass, which passed material to it as an asymptotic giant. The level of niobium suggests that the transfer happened more than three million years ago. The two orbit every 6.5 years.

hip-82363.name: Eta Arae
hip-82363.introduction: is an orange giant in Ara, about 305 light-years away, 40 times the Sun’s radius.

sections.title: A very slow spin
sections.text: About five billion years old, with 1.1 times the Sun’s mass, it now rotates so slowly that one turn takes more than eleven years.

msc-07087-7030.name: Gamma Volantis
msc-07087-7030.introduction: is a double star in Volans, about 133 light-years away and 9 degrees from the Large Magellanic Cloud.

sections.title: An orange and a yellow-white star
sections.text: The brighter star, Gamma² Volantis, is an orange giant and the brightest star in Volans; Gamma¹ is a yellow-white main-sequence star. Their separation has slowly shrunk from 15.7 arcseconds in 1826 to 14.1 in 2002.

hip-87585.name: Grumium
hip-87585.introduction: is Xi Draconis, an orange giant in Draco, about 112 light-years away. Its name is a corruption of the Latin grunnum, “snout,” because Ptolemy placed it on the dragon’s jaw.

sections.title: One of the Mother Camels
sections.text: With Rastaban, Eltanin, Alrakis and Kuma, it formed the Arabic asterism of the Mother Camels. A faint star 316 arcseconds away may be a companion: Gaia shows a similar distance and motion.

spectroscopic-hip-23453.name: Saclateni
spectroscopic-hip-23453.introduction: is Zeta Aurigae, an eclipsing binary about 860 light-years away and one of the “kids” of the she-goat Capella.

sections.title: An eclipse every 2.7 years
sections.text: An orange bright giant and a hot blue-white star orbit every 972 days. When the giant passes in front, the blue star disappears; Harper noticed the vanishing spectrum in 1924, and the eclipses were confirmed in 1932. The dimming is much deeper in ultraviolet than in visible light.

hip-95853.name: Iota² Cygni
hip-95853.introduction: is a white star in Cygnus, about 121 light-years away.

sections.title: A spinning star with a disk
sections.text: About 577 million years old, it spins at about 240 km/s. Rapid changes in a calcium absorption line suggest a disk of gas around it. It is approaching and should pass within about 92 light-years in some 783,000 years.

hip-41312.name: Beta Volantis
hip-41312.introduction: is an orange giant in Volans, about 108 light-years away.

sections.title: Weighed by its oscillations
sections.text: Asteroseismology gives it about 1.6 times the Sun’s mass. It fuses helium in its core and has expanded to 10 times the Sun’s radius.

hip-80170.name: Gamma Herculis
hip-80170.introduction: is a white giant in Hercules, about 193 light-years away, also known as Hejian.

sections.title: A slowly varying giant
sections.text: Spinning at about 135 km/s, it has expanded to about six times the Sun’s radius. Small, slow brightness changes repeat roughly every half year.

hip-26069.name: Beta Doradus
hip-26069.introduction: is a yellow supergiant in Dorado, about 1,040 light-years away, and one of the brightest Cepheid variables.

sections.title: A pulsating supergiant
sections.text: Its brightness rises and falls between magnitudes 3.46 and 4.08 in a regular saw-tooth pattern, while its radius swings by about 3.9 solar radii around 68. Its X-ray emission varies in step with the pulsation.

hip-94779.name: Kappa Cygni
hip-94779.introduction: is a yellow giant at the tip of the swan’s left wing, about 123 light-years away.

sections.title: A meteor shower’s neighbor
sections.text: The radiant of the minor Kappa Cygnid meteor shower lies about 5 degrees north. The star is only 880 million years old but has already become a giant because massive stars evolve faster.

hip-20455.name: Secunda Hyadum
hip-20455.introduction: is Delta¹ Tauri, a member of the Hyades, the nearest open cluster.

sections.title: On the Moon’s path
sections.text: With Delta² and Delta³ Tauri, it forms a small group of Hyades stars near the ecliptic, so they can be occulted by the Moon and, very rarely, by planets.

hip-102618.name: Albali
hip-102618.introduction: is Epsilon Aquarii, a white star about 244 light-years away. Its name comes from the Arabic for “the swallower.”

sections.title: A companion found in 2023
sections.text: Observations with ESO telescopes revealed in 2023 that it is a binary: an orange dwarf orbits the primary every 1.2 years, about 1.7 AU away. The primary has three times the Sun’s mass and has just left the main sequence.

hip-111169.name: Stellio
hip-111169.introduction: is Alpha Lacertae, the brightest star in Lacerta, about 103 light-years away. Stellio was an old name for the constellation, after the starred agama lizard.

sections.title: An ordinary young star
sections.text: About 400 million years old, with 2.2 times the Sun’s mass, it spins at about 128 km/s. Its faint visual companion is a chance alignment.

hip-93683.name: Alqiladah
hip-93683.introduction: is Omicron Sagittarii, a yellow giant about 142 light-years away, which came within 86 light-years of the Sun about a million years ago.

sections.title: Near the Sun’s path
sections.text: Lying near the ecliptic, it can be occulted by the Moon and planets: Mercury last covered it on December 24, 1937. It fuses helium in its core and is about 2.4 billion years old.

orb6-14411+1344-a-b.name: Zeta Boötis
orb6-14411+1344-a-b.introduction: is a pair of white stars in Boötes, about 180 light-years away, on one of the most eccentric orbits known.

sections.title: A plunging orbit
sections.text: The two nearly identical stars orbit every 125 years on an extremely elongated path, with an eccentricity of 0.98, closing to just 0.82 AU at their last closest approach in November 2023. A distant third star, about 41,000 AU away, probably forced the pair into this orbit. Stable planetary orbits are unlikely in such a system.

hip-13268.name: Miram
hip-13268.introduction: is Eta Persei, an orange supergiant about 1,000 light-years away, part of the Segment of Perseus. The name Miram appeared in the 20th century from an unknown source.

sections.title: An enormous star
sections.text: It has expanded to 170 times the Sun’s size and shines 7,500 times as brightly. Of its catalogued companions, only an 8th-magnitude star 28 arcseconds away seems to lie at the same distance.

hip-53253.name: u Carinae
hip-53253.introduction: is HD 94510, an orange star in Carina, about 95 light-years away, near the border with Vela.

sections.title: A giant in the making
sections.text: It is evolving into a giant, with 1.9 times the Sun’s mass and 6.9 times its radius, and may vary slightly.

hip-34088.name: Mekbuda
hip-34088.introduction: is Zeta Geminorum, a Cepheid variable about 1,200 light-years away. Its name comes from the Arabic for “the lion’s folded paw.”

sections.title: A ruler for the cosmos
sections.text: Its regular pulsations make it a calibrator for the cosmic distance ladder. W. W. Campbell found in 1899 that its velocity changes, which turned out to be pulsation rather than orbital motion, and Paul Guthnick noticed in 1920 that its period itself changes.

hip-36046.name: Iota Geminorum
hip-36046.introduction: is a yellow giant in Gemini that forms an isosceles triangle with Castor and Pollux.

sections.title: A giant
sections.text: With 1.9 times the Sun’s mass, it has expanded to 9.5 times the Sun’s radius. It has sometimes been called Propus, a name that belongs more correctly to Eta Geminorum.

hip-112961.name: Shatabhisha
hip-112961.introduction: is Lambda Aquarii, a red giant about 365 light-years away. Its name is that of an Indian nakshatra meaning “a hundred physicians.”

sections.title: Close to the ecliptic
sections.text: Lying just 0.39 degrees from the ecliptic, it is often occulted by the Moon, and Venus covered it on April 16, 2014. A faint companion was found during a lunar occultation in 2016.

sections.title: A large, slow pulsator
sections.text: An asymptotic giant with 3.6 times the Sun’s mass and 100 times its radius, it varies irregularly with several periods of 24 to 50 days.

hip-72370.name: Paradys
hip-72370.introduction: is Alpha Apodis, the brightest star in Apus, the bird of paradise, about 500 light-years away. Its name comes from the original Dutch name of the constellation, Paradys-vogel.

sections.title: Finding the bird
sections.text: A line from Alpha Centauri through Alpha Circini points to it. It is an orange giant 65 times the Sun’s radius, shining 1,000 times as brightly.

spectroscopic-hip-97804.name: Eta Aquilae
spectroscopic-hip-97804.introduction: is a Cepheid variable in Aquila, about 890 light-years away, whose brightness swings between magnitudes 3.49 and 4.3 every 7.18 days.

sections.title: Companions of a Cepheid
sections.text: A faint hot companion shows up in ultraviolet light, and another star 0.7 arcseconds away appears to be bound, taking at least 659 years per orbit. Eta Aquilae once belonged to the obsolete constellation Antinous.

msc-15348+1032.name: Delta Serpentis
msc-15348+1032.introduction: is a multiple star in Serpens Caput, about 230 light-years away.

sections.title: Pairs on two scales
sections.text: The primary, a yellow-white subgiant and Delta Scuti variable, has a close partner on a 265-day orbit. A second subgiant, four arcseconds away, circles them every 3,200 years.

msc-20396+1555.name: Sualocin
msc-20396+1555.introduction: is Alpha Delphini, the dolphin’s brightest star after Rotanev, about 238 light-years away.

sections.title: A joke in the catalog
sections.text: Sualocin is “Nicolaus,” Rotanev is “Venator,” reversed: the Latinized name of Niccolò Cacciatore, Giuseppe Piazzi’s assistant, who slipped them into the Palermo Star Catalogue of 1814.

sections.title: A triple star
sections.text: The primary, a subgiant with 3.8 times the Sun’s mass, has a companion 0.2 arcseconds away on a 17-year orbit; that companion is itself a 30-day binary.

hip-86414.name: Iota Herculis
hip-86414.introduction: is a blue-white subgiant in Hercules, about 455 light-years away, also named Tianbang. It was the north pole star around 10,000 BCE and will be again.

sections.title: A pulsating star
sections.text: It is a Beta Cephei variable with 5.4 times the Sun’s mass, 2,500 times as luminous, with an unseen companion. A star once thought to be a distant companion is, according to Gaia, much farther away.

hip-48319.name: Upsilon Ursae Majoris
hip-48319.introduction: is a yellow-white subgiant in Ursa Major, about 246 light-years away, with a faint companion.

sections.title: A quick pulse
sections.text: It is a Delta Scuti variable pulsing every 3.2 hours and spins about once every 1.2 days. A red dwarf 11.8 arcseconds away has about 40% of the Sun’s mass.

hip-51232.name: s Carinae
hip-51232.introduction: is S Carinae, a Mira variable in Carina, about 1,620 light-years away, discovered by Benjamin Gould in 1871.

sections.title: A hot Mira
sections.text: Its brightness swings between magnitudes 4.5 and 10.0 every 150 days, visible to the eye only near maximum. It has one of the hottest spectra and shortest periods of any Mira variable.

spectroscopic-hip-97365.name: Delta Sagittae
spectroscopic-hip-97365.introduction: is a binary in Sagitta, about 430 light-years away, combining a red bright giant and a hot blue-white star. Its proper name is Zuoqi.

sections.title: A red and blue pair
sections.text: Light from both stars shows in the spectrum. They orbit every 10 years, and the system varies unpredictably between magnitudes 3.75 and 3.83.

hip-51069.name: Mu Hydrae
hip-51069.introduction: is an orange giant in Hydra, about 234 light-years away, 45 times the Sun’s radius.

sections.title: A planetary nebula nearby
sections.text: The planetary nebula NGC 3242 lies just 1.8 degrees to the south-southwest.

orb6-15427+2618-a-b.name: Gamma Coronae Borealis
orb6-15427+2618-a-b.introduction: is a pair of white stars in the Northern Crown, about 146 light-years away, orbiting every 91 years.

sections.title: A puzzling variable
sections.text: The primary varies on timescales of about 43 minutes, with no known mechanism for a star of its temperature. It is one of the stars that defined the Maia variables, a class that may hardly exist.

hip-35037.name: Omega Canis Majoris
hip-35037.introduction: is a blue-white Be star in Canis Major, about 920 light-years away, one of the most observed Be stars of the southern sky.

sections.title: A pole-on spinner
sections.text: We see it nearly pole-on, so although it appears to rotate at 80 km/s, its equator moves at about 350 km/s. It varies between magnitudes 3.6 and 4.2 with periods near 1.4 days and is surrounded by a disk of gas.

msc-02020+0246.name: Alrescha
msc-02020+0246.introduction: is Alpha Piscium, a triple star about 157 light-years away. Its name comes from the Arabic for “the cord.”

sections.title: A slow orbit
sections.text: Alrescha A and a close pair, B, orbit each other every 2,800 years and will be closest around 2188; the B stars circle each other every 25 days. A Sun-like star nearly 7 arcminutes away may make it a four-star system.

hip-21393.name: Theemin
hip-21393.introduction: is Upsilon² Eridani, a yellow giant about 211 light-years away.

sections.title: A name that changed in translation
sections.text: Ptolemy called it “the bend in the river.” Arab writers corrupted the Greek into bhmn, which became Beemin in the West, and later Theemin, wrongly derived from the Hebrew for “twins.”

hip-88794.name: Omicron Herculis
hip-88794.introduction: is a blue-white star in Hercules near the solar apex, the point in the sky toward which the Sun is moving. William Herschel noticed this direction in 1783.

sections.title: A future brightest star
sections.text: In about 3.47 million years, it will be the brightest star in the night sky, at magnitude −0.63. It is a fast-spinning, mass-losing Gamma Cassiopeiae variable that has just left the main sequence.

hip-91117.name: Alpha Scuti
hip-91117.introduction: is the brightest star in Scutum, an orange giant about 199 light-years away. Its proper name is Tianbian.

sections.title: An inflated giant
sections.text: With 1.3 times the Sun’s mass, it has expanded to 20 times the Sun’s radius.

hip-53229.name: Praecipua
hip-53229.introduction: is 46 Leonis Minoris, the brightest star in Leo Minor, about 99 light-years away. Its name is Latin for “the chief one.”

sections.title: The alpha that never was
sections.text: Francis Baily set out to letter every star of Leo Minor brighter than magnitude 4.5, yet his catalog left this one, the brightest, without a Greek letter, even though the dimmer Beta was included. It is a red clump giant.

hip-54463.name: x Carinae
hip-54463.introduction: is V382 Carinae, a yellow hypergiant about 8,560 light-years away and some 320,000 times as luminous as the Sun.

sections.title: A giant at a crossroads
sections.text: With about 620 times the Sun’s radius, its surface would reach into the asteroid belt if placed at the Sun. Its low infrared excess suggests it is cooling toward a red supergiant phase. It varies irregularly, a supergiant pulsating like an irregular Cepheid.

msc-03442-6448.name: Beta Reticuli
msc-03442-6448.introduction: is an orange giant in Reticulum, about 101 light-years away, with a red-dwarf companion on a 5.25-year orbit.

sections.title: A fast traveler
sections.text: Between 5 and 6 billion years old, it moves at about 69 km/s relative to the Sun. It came closest about 319,000 years ago, 67 light-years away and shining at magnitude 3.0. A Sun-like star once proposed as a third member turned out to be unrelated.

hip-110395.name: Sadachbia
hip-110395.introduction: is Gamma Aquarii, a white star in the Water Jar of Aquarius, about 164 light-years away. Its name comes from the Arabic for “luck of the tents.”

sections.title: A companion found in 2024
sections.text: Listed as a spectroscopic binary, then as single, it was finally shown in 2024 by interferometry to have an orange companion, about 1.9 AU away, orbiting about once a year. The companion probably explains the X-rays seen from the system.

msc-04287+1552.name: Theta¹ Tauri
msc-04287+1552.introduction: is an orange giant in the Hyades, about 152 light-years away, and the fainter star of the naked-eye pair Theta Tauri.

sections.title: A giant with a companion
sections.text: A seventh-magnitude companion of about 1.3 solar masses orbits it every 16.3 years on an eccentric path. Its naked-eye neighbor, Chamukuy (Theta² Tauri), lies 5.6 arcminutes away.

hip-78072.name: Gamma Serpentis
hip-78072.introduction: is a yellow-white star in Serpens Caput, about 36 light-years away. Its proper name, Muning, is the Wardaman name for the small rock cod.

sections.title: A slightly larger Sun
sections.text: About 3.5 billion years old, it is 21% more massive and 44% larger than the Sun, and nearly three times as luminous.

msc-10373-4814.name: p Velorum
msc-10373-4814.introduction: is a triple star in Vela, about 88 light-years away.

sections.title: Three stars
sections.text: Two yellow-white stars orbit every 10.2 days, and a white star 0.36 arcseconds away circles them every 16.7 years.

hip-30277.name: Delta Columbae
hip-30277.introduction: is a yellow bright giant in Columba, about 217 light-years away, formerly listed as 3 Canis Majoris.

sections.title: A possible runaway binary
sections.text: An unseen companion orbits every 869 days on an elongated path. Its speed relative to its surroundings makes the system a candidate runaway.

hip-27654.name: Delta Leporis
hip-27654.introduction: is an old orange giant in Lepus, about 114 light-years away and about 10.7 billion years old.

sections.title: A Population II star
sections.text: It is an old Population II star, poor in iron, with 94% of the Sun’s mass and ten times its radius.

hip-50191.name: q Velorum
hip-50191.introduction: is HD 88955, a white star in Vela, about 103 light-years away, a probable member of the Argus Association.

sections.title: A debris disk
sections.text: About 410 million years old, it has a debris disk about 19 AU from the star.

hip-56211.name: Giausar
hip-56211.introduction: is Lambda Draconis, a red giant in Draco, about 333 light-years away. Its name comes from a Persian term for the nodes of the Moon’s orbit.

sections.title: An old red giant
sections.text: On the asymptotic giant branch, it has a radius 70 times the Sun’s and may vary slowly over about 1,100 days.

hip-89341.name: Polis
hip-89341.introduction: is Mu Sagittarii, a blue supergiant about 5,000 light-years away in the Sgr OB1 association. Its name comes from the Greek for “city,” the name of a lunar station.

sections.title: A massive eclipsing pair
sections.text: The supergiant, about 23 times the Sun’s mass and wider than Mercury’s orbit, is eclipsed every 181 days by a hot companion. It will probably end as a supernova. Fainter stars nearby may form a loose trapezium-like group.

hip-81065.name: Gamma Apodis
hip-81065.introduction: is a yellow giant in Apus, about 153 light-years away.

sections.title: An X-ray-bright giant
sections.text: It fuses helium in its core and is one of the 100 strongest stellar X-ray sources within 50 parsecs of the Sun.

hip-27321.name: Beta Pictoris
hip-27321.introduction: is a young white star in Pictor, about 63 light-years away and only about 23 million years old. It was the first star whose debris disk was imaged.

sections.title: Three planets in a disk
sections.text: Three planets, b, c and d, orbit in the plane of its dusty disk; Beta Pictoris c is the closest planet to its star ever photographed, at roughly the distance of the asteroid belt from the Sun. Belts of planetesimals and comets suggest that planets may still be forming.

sections.title: A source of interstellar meteoroids
sections.text: Material from its disk is thought to be the main source of interstellar meteoroids reaching the Solar System. The star gives its name to the Beta Pictoris moving group of young stars.

hip-19747.name: Alpha Horologii
hip-19747.introduction: is the brightest star in Horologium, an orange giant about 118 light-years away.

sections.title: A former white star
sections.text: About 3.6 billion years old, it spent most of its life as a white main-sequence star before swelling to about ten times the Sun’s diameter.

hip-79992.name: Tau Herculis
hip-79992.introduction: is a blue-white star in Hercules, about 307 light-years away. Its proper name, Asuusiha, is a Manchu constellation representing a net used to hunt sables.

sections.title: A past and future pole star
sections.text: Tau Herculis may have served as the north pole star around 7400 BCE and will again around the year 18,400. Only 26 million years old, it is a slowly pulsating B star discovered by Hipparcos.

hip-17573.name: Maia
hip-17573.introduction: is the fourth-brightest star of the Pleiades, named after one of the seven daughters of Atlas and Pleione. It lights up NGC 1432, the Maia Nebula, one of the brightest reflection nebulae in the cluster.

sections.title: The star behind a variable class
sections.text: Otto Struve thought Maia was variable and proposed a class of Maia variables. Hipparcos found no such variability, but Kepler later saw small changes every 10.3 days, attributed to a rotating starspot. It is a chemically peculiar blue giant, weak in helium and rich in manganese.

hip-765.name: Epsilon Phoenicis
hip-765.introduction: is an orange giant in Phoenix, about 144 light-years away.

sections.title: A helium-burning giant
sections.text: About twice the Sun’s mass, it has passed through a helium flash and now fuses helium in its core, at ten times the Sun’s radius.

msc-04382-1418.name: Sceptrum
msc-04382-1418.introduction: is 53 Eridani, a binary about 110 light-years away. Its Latin name, “scepter,” comes from Sceptrum Brandenburgicum, an obsolete constellation honoring the Brandenburg province of Prussia.

sections.title: A giant and its partner
sections.text: An orange giant and a 7th-magnitude companion orbit each other every 77 years on an eccentric path.

hip-33152.name: Omicron¹ Canis Majoris
hip-33152.introduction: is a red supergiant in Canis Major, roughly 2,700 light-years away, about 390 times the Sun’s diameter and 37,000 times as luminous.

sections.title: A future supernova
sections.text: About 18 million years old, with around 8 times the Sun’s mass, it fuses helium in its core and will one day explode as a supernova. It is linked with the Collinder 121 association, although its distance is uncertain; it is unrelated to Omicron² Canis Majoris, 2 degrees away.

hip-68282.name: Upsilon¹ Centauri
hip-68282.introduction: is a hot blue-white star in Centaurus, about 427 light-years away, in the Lower Centaurus–Crux group.

sections.title: A young massive star
sections.text: Only 13 million years old, with 7.9 times the Sun’s mass, it radiates about 1,900 times the Sun’s light.

hip-25859.name: Epsilon Columbae
hip-25859.introduction: is an orange giant in Columba, about 278 light-years away.

sections.title: A possible runaway
sections.text: About 1.5 billion years old, with 2.5 times the Sun’s mass and 25 times its radius, it moves fast enough to be a runaway candidate. Changes in its motion reveal an unseen companion.

hip-4436.name: Mu Andromedae
hip-4436.introduction: is a white star about 122 light-years away, halfway between Mirach and the Andromeda Galaxy in the sky.

sections.title: Spun up by a partner
sections.text: In 2007 it was found to be a tidally locked binary with an unseen companion orbiting every 551 days. The tides have spun up the primary, making it magnetically active with unusually strong starspots.

hip-13701.name: Azha
hip-13701.introduction: is Eta Eridani, an orange giant about 137 light-years away. Its name comes from a miscopied Arabic word for “the ostrich nest.”

sections.title: A barium star without a partner
sections.text: A red clump giant fusing helium in its core, it is a mild barium star. Most barium stars are binaries, but Azha has no known companion.

hip-114421.name: Iota Gruis
hip-114421.introduction: is an orange giant in Grus, about 183 light-years away.

sections.title: An eccentric partner
sections.text: An unseen companion orbits it every 410 days on a very eccentric path.

hip-48455.name: Rasalas
hip-48455.introduction: is Mu Leonis, an orange giant about 124 light-years away in the lion’s head. Its name comes from the Arabic for “the northern lion’s head.”

sections.title: A giant with a planet
sections.text: About 5 billion years old, older than the Sun, it has a diameter 11.7 times the Sun’s, measured by the CHARA array. A planet found in 2014 has, according to Gaia astrometry, at most about 12.6 Jupiter masses, so it is a planet rather than a brown dwarf.

msc-19563+3505.name: Eta Cygni
msc-19563+3505.introduction: is an orange giant in Cygnus, about 139 light-years away, midway between Sadr and Albireo.

sections.title: A helium-burning giant
sections.text: It fuses helium in its core and has expanded to ten times the Sun’s radius. Of five visual companions, only a 12th-magnitude star 7.8 arcseconds away seems physically associated.

hip-87808.name: Theta Herculis
hip-87808.introduction: is an orange bright giant in Hercules, about 750 light-years away, rich in cyanogen.

sections.title: A variable giant
sections.text: Its variability was noticed in 1935. Only 130 million years old, with 5.9 times the Sun’s mass, it has expanded to 82 times the Sun’s radius.

spectroscopic-hip-61199.name: Gamma Muscae
spectroscopic-hip-61199.introduction: is a blue-white star in Musca, about 325 light-years away, in the Lower Centaurus–Crux association.

sections.title: A slowly pulsating B star
sections.text: With about five times the Sun’s mass, it varies slightly every 2.7 days and spins at about 205 km/s, bulging 7% at the equator.

msc-14431-0540.name: Mu Virginis
msc-14431-0540.introduction: is a yellow-white star in Virgo, about 60 light-years away, near the celestial equator.

sections.title: A possible distant partner
sections.text: About 1.5 billion years old, it spins at about 47 km/s. A faint star about 770 AU away may share its motion.

spectroscopic-hip-8832.name: Mesarthim
spectroscopic-hip-8832.introduction: is Gamma Arietis, a double star about 166 light-years away, once called “the first star in Aries” as the nearest visible star to the spring equinox point.

sections.title: Twin white stars
sections.text: A small telescope splits it into two nearly equal white stars, 7.6 arcseconds apart, orbiting every 6,600 years or so. One is a magnetic, chemically peculiar star whose brightness changes as it rotates; the other is a fast-spinning Lambda Boötis star.

orb6-13310-3924-a-b.name: d Centauri
orb6-13310-3924-a-b.introduction: is HD 117440, a pair of yellow giants in Centaurus, about 900 light-years away.

sections.title: Two giants
sections.text: T. J. J. See first reported the companion in 1897; the two giants orbit every 83 years.

spectroscopic-hip-45336.name: Theta Hydrae
spectroscopic-hip-45336.introduction: is a white star in Hydra, about 115 light-years away, with a white dwarf companion.

sections.title: An unusually heavy white dwarf
sections.text: The companion was discovered from its X-rays in 1998. One estimate gives it 1.21 solar masses, which would be beyond the upper limit for white dwarfs from typical single stars.

orb6-12335+6947-a-b.name: Kappa Draconis
orb6-12335+6947-a-b.introduction: is a blue-white Be star in Draco, about 460 light-years away, five times the Sun’s mass.

sections.title: A pole star of the second millennium BC
sections.text: From 1793 BC to about 1000 BC it was the nearest naked-eye star to the north celestial pole, though 6 degrees away. It has a subdwarf companion on a 61.6-day orbit and is just entering its red giant phase.

orb6-19482+7016-a-b.name: Tyl
orb6-19482+7016-a-b.introduction: is Epsilon Draconis, a yellow giant about 150 light-years away. With Altais and two other stars, it formed the Arabic asterism of the Goat.

sections.title: A giant and a sunny companion
sections.text: A red clump giant with about half the Sun’s metal content, it has a yellow-white companion 3.2 arcseconds away, about 145 AU in projection.

hip-60823.name: Sigma Centauri
hip-60823.introduction: is a hot blue-white star in Centaurus, about 412 light-years away, rich in helium.

sections.title: A helium-rich star
sections.text: Helium-rich stars are the most massive type of chemically peculiar star. Sigma Centauri has about 6.8 times the Sun’s mass and is about 25 million years old.

hip-31592.name: Nu² Canis Majoris
hip-31592.introduction: is an orange giant near Sirius, about 67 light-years away, with two known planets.

sections.title: Planets in resonance
sections.text: A planet of at least 2.6 Jupiter masses orbits every 2.1 years, and a second, found by 2019, is locked with it in a 4:3 resonance. The star is about 4.6 billion years old and has not yet undergone its helium flash.

msc-03443+3217.name: Atik
msc-03443+3217.introduction: is Omicron Persei, a triple star about 1,100 light-years away, just north of the young cluster IC 348. Its name comes from the Arabic for “the shoulder.”

sections.title: A distorted pair
sections.text: Two hot stars only about 33 solar radii apart distort each other into egg shapes, so the system varies as they orbit.

hip-76333.name: Zubenelhakrabi
hip-76333.introduction: is Gamma Librae, a yellow giant about 163 light-years away. Its name means “the claws of the scorpion,” from before Libra was separated from Scorpius.

sections.title: Two planets in resonance
sections.text: Two gas giants of at least 1.0 and 4.6 Jupiter masses orbit every 415 and 965 days, in a 7:3 resonance.

msc-09188+3648.name: 38 Lyncis
msc-09188+3648.introduction: is a multiple star in Lynx, about 125 light-years away: a blue-white star with a fainter companion that has been described as lilac.

sections.title: A double within a double
sections.text: The pair is 2.6 arcseconds apart and takes about 429 years per orbit; the fainter star is itself a close binary on a 2.1-year orbit. When the Morgan–Keenan system was defined in 1943, 38 Lyncis served as a standard for class A3 V.

msc-17003+3056.name: Epsilon Herculis
msc-17003+3056.introduction: is a white star in Hercules, about 155 light-years away, whose multiplicity is still debated.

sections.title: A hippopotamus’s buttocks
sections.text: In the Ramesside star clocks of ancient Egypt, it was Khepdenreret, the buttocks of the hippopotamus goddess Reret. Catalogs list it variously as single, double and triple.

hip-21444.name: Nu Eridani
hip-21444.introduction: is a hot blue-white subgiant in Eridanus, about 520 light-years away. At 33 light-years, it would outshine Sirius.

sections.title: A hybrid pulsator
sections.text: Robert Baker discovered its variability in 1926. It shows at least fourteen pulsation frequencies, lying where Beta Cephei variables and slowly pulsating B stars overlap.

hip-95168.name: Rho¹ Sagittarii
hip-95168.introduction: is a white subgiant in Sagittarius, about 127 light-years away, close enough to the ecliptic to be occulted by the Moon.

sections.title: An Egyptian decan
sections.text: Kenemu, the 17th decan of ancient Egyptian astronomy, was a small group of stars around Rho¹ Sagittarii. The star itself is a Delta Scuti variable.

hip-112440.name: Lambda Pegasi
hip-112440.introduction: is a yellow giant in Pegasus, about 365 light-years away. Its proper name is Ligong.

sections.title: A line-of-sight double
sections.text: It appears close to Mu Pegasi, with which it shared the Arabic name Sadalbari, but it lies about three times farther away.

hip-37447.name: Alpha Monocerotis
hip-37447.introduction: is a yellow giant in Monoceros, about 146 light-years away. Despite its alpha designation, Beta Monocerotis is brighter.

sections.title: A helium-burning giant
sections.text: About 890 million years old, it fuses helium in its core and rotates about once every 326 days.

spectroscopic-hip-104987.name: Kitalpha
spectroscopic-hip-104987.introduction: is Alpha Equulei, the brightest star in Equuleus. Its name comes from the Arabic for “a piece of the horse.”

sections.title: A giant and an Am star
sections.text: A yellow giant and a white Am star orbit every 98.8 days on a circular path, with masses of 2.2 and 1.9 Suns.

hip-7083.name: Delta Phoenicis
hip-7083.introduction: is a yellow giant in Phoenix, about 142 light-years away.

sections.title: A helium-burning giant
sections.text: About 2.3 billion years old, it fuses helium in its core.

hip-2072.name: Kappa Phoenicis
hip-2072.introduction: is a white star in Phoenix, about 78 light-years away, a member of the Castor Moving Group.

sections.title: A spinning star with a disk
sections.text: It spins at about 245 km/s and shows a debris disk about 9 AU from the star.

hip-42911.name: Asellus Australis
hip-42911.introduction: is Delta Cancri, an orange giant about 137 light-years away. Its name means “southern donkey colt”; with Asellus Borealis it flanks the Beehive Cluster.

sections.title: A weather sign
sections.text: Aratus wrote that if the northern donkey colt is hidden by haze while the southern one shines, a south wind will blow. The Babylonians made it the 13th ecliptic station, and it was involved in the first recorded occultation by Jupiter, reported by Ptolemy for September 3, 240 BC. Lying just 0.08 degrees from the ecliptic, it is still occulted by the Moon.

hip-98495.name: Epsilon Pavonis
hip-98495.introduction: is a white star in Pavo, about 105 light-years away and only about 27 million years old.

sections.title: A young star
sections.text: It belongs to the proposed Argus Association, a young group of more than 60 stars linked to IC 2391.

hip-95347.name: Rukbat
hip-95347.introduction: is Alpha Sagittarii, a blue-white star in the archer’s knee; its name comes from the Arabic for “the knee of the archer.”

sections.title: An alpha that is not the brightest
sections.text: It is unclear why Bayer made it alpha, since Kaus Australis and Nunki are at least five times brighter. Excess infrared suggests a debris disk, and unexpected X-rays point to a young companion.

hip-37504.name: Zeta Volantis
hip-37504.introduction: is an orange giant in Volans, about 145 light-years away, with a 9.7-magnitude companion.

sections.title: A past visitor
sections.text: About 858,000 years ago, the system passed within 22 light-years of the Sun; it is now receding at 48 km/s.

msc-15509-3338.name: Chi Lupi
msc-15509-3338.introduction: is a triple star in Lupus, in the Upper Scorpius association.

sections.title: Peculiar partners
sections.text: The primary is a mercury-manganese star, its companion a metallic-line star, and a red dwarf completes the trio.

hip-42515.name: Beta Pyxidis
hip-42515.introduction: is a yellow giant in Pyxis, about 420 light-years away, the second-brightest star in the constellation.

sections.title: Did it swallow a planet?
sections.text: It spins unusually fast for an evolved giant, at about 12 km/s. One possible explanation is that it engulfed a giant planet such as a hot Jupiter.

hip-20535.name: Beemim
hip-20535.introduction: is Upsilon³ Eridani, an orange giant about 296 light-years away, 54 times the Sun’s radius.

sections.title: A borrowed name
sections.text: Its name is a variant of Theemin, the traditional name of its neighbor Upsilon² Eridani.

spectroscopic-hip-44248.name: 10 Ursae Majoris
spectroscopic-hip-44248.introduction: is a binary about 53 light-years away, now in Lynx, the third-brightest object in that constellation. John Flamsteed wrongly placed it in Ursa Major, hence its name.

sections.title: A Sun-like pair
sections.text: A yellow-white star and an orange dwarf orbit every 21 years. The system is a probable member of the Hyades supercluster.

hip-28328.name: Eta Columbae
hip-28328.introduction: is an orange giant in Columba, about 441 light-years away.

sections.title: A large giant
sections.text: With 4.7 times the Sun’s mass, it has expanded to 36 times the Sun’s radius.

hip-29651.name: Gamma Monocerotis
hip-29651.introduction: is an orange giant in Monoceros, about 500 light-years away.

sections.title: Barium from a dead partner
sections.text: It is a mild barium star: heavy elements were deposited by a companion during its asymptotic-giant-branch phase, and that companion is now a white dwarf.

hip-110997.name: Delta¹ Gruis
hip-110997.introduction: is a yellow giant in Grus, about 309 light-years away, which varies semiregularly between magnitudes 3.99 and 4.2.

sections.title: A giant and a faint companion
sections.text: With about three times the Sun’s mass, it has a 12.8-magnitude companion 5.6 arcseconds away.

hip-112716.name: Lintangkumba
hip-112716.introduction: is Tau² Aquarii, an orange giant about 326 light-years away. Its name is the Balinese name for Aquarius, from lintang, “constellation,” and Kumbha.

sections.title: Herschel’s companion
sections.text: William Herschel reported a faint visual companion in 1782. The star lies near the ecliptic and can be occulted by the Moon.

msc-23174-5814.name: Gamma Tucanae
msc-23174-5814.introduction: is a yellow-white star in Tucana, about 75 light-years away.

sections.title: A distant companion?
sections.text: About 1.4 billion years old, it is a suspected astrometric binary and may have a distant, Sun-like companion, HD 223913, about 11 light-years away.

msc-03121-2859.name: Dalim
msc-03121-2859.introduction: is Alpha Fornacis, the only star in Fornax brighter than magnitude 4, about 46 light-years away.

sections.title: A blue straggler and a close encounter
sections.text: Its companion, B, is a blue straggler that probably gained mass from a third star, detected in 2016. About 350,000 years ago, Alpha Fornacis passed only about 0.27 light-years from Nu Horologii, and both stars have debris disks.

hip-115438.name: 98 Aquarii
hip-115438.introduction: is an orange giant in Aquarius, about 163 light-years away, about 14 times the Sun’s radius.

sections.title: An evolved giant
sections.text: With more than twice the Sun’s mass, it has exhausted the hydrogen in its core.

orb6-09024-6624-a-b.name: Alpha Volantis
orb6-09024-6624-a-b.introduction: is a pair of white stars in Volans, about 125 light-years away, a member of the Sirius supercluster.

sections.title: A close pair
sections.text: The two nearly equal stars are only 0.03 arcseconds apart. The primary is an Am star about 427 million years old.

hip-35228.name: Delta Volantis
hip-35228.introduction: is a yellow-white bright giant in Volans, about 740 light-years away.

sections.title: A luminous giant
sections.text: With five times the Sun’s mass and 36 times its radius, it shines more than 1,000 times as brightly.

hip-10670.name: Apdu
hip-10670.introduction: is Gamma Trianguli, a white star about 112 light-years away. Its name comes from Apdu, “the Bird,” an ancient Egyptian constellation between Algol and Triangulum.

sections.title: A spinning star with a ring
sections.text: Its spectral lines are very diffuse because it spins rapidly. A ring of cold dust, about 80 AU from the star, glows in infrared light. It forms a line-of-sight triple with Delta and 7 Trianguli.

hip-22109.name: Mu Eridani
hip-22109.introduction: is an eclipsing binary in Eridanus, about 520 light-years away.

sections.title: Pulsations and eclipses
sections.text: Its binary nature was found in 1910; a companion orbits every 7.4 days. The primary’s pulsations were detected in 2004, and eclipses in 2005.
